text: To require the Czech authorities: to take corrective measures as regards observed deficiencies in particular the Czech approval procedure for meat product export establishments and its implementation, and to approve the establishments for export to the Member States of the Community accordingly;
To require the Czech authorities to inform the Commission's service of these corrective measures;
To list the Czech meat product establishments proposed by the Czech authorities on the basis of the above mentioned;
To require the Czech authorities to inform the Commission about full implementation of the HACCP system;
To perform a follow up mission in the Czech Republic after receiving the information on implementation of the HACCP system.

There are deficiencies in the execution of local movement in the protected zones. The Portuguese authorities are requested to make the execution coherent with the provisions laid down in Council Directive 77/93/EEC. Deficiencies were found on the Azores. As the visits were limited to the Azores and the region Ribatejo e Oeste, it is recommended that, when a similar situation occurs in other regions in Portugal, the recommendations should also apply to those regions.

Regarding the return of soil to the production fields of sugar beets, it is recommended that the DSPPA takes measures to ensure that the soil is returned to the field from which it originates. This limits the risk of Rhizomania spreading in the event of late discovery.
DGPC is urged to carry out an investigation, if necessary in co-operation with the DRA's, to the extend local movement is applied in Portugal (see conclusion 6.4). 5

There are deficiencies in the execution of local movement in the protected zones, as referred to in § 7.4. The Spanish authorities are requested to take the necessary measures to make the execution coherent with the provisions laid down in Council Directive 77/93/EEC. For the fire blight host plants this means that the plants need to be accompanied by a plant passport when sold from a garden centre to the final consumer. This recommendation should be implemented as early as is practicable. In EC legislation

The basic rules for local movement are laid down in Council Directive 77/93/EEC. There is a need for more clear definitions and rules by the service of the Commission in charge of legislation on plant health. Elements and proposals with regard to this were discussed during the mission. 5

The system laid down in the Decision can not function, as long as the separation of lots already from the beginning onwards is not ensured. Numbered labels and colour codes facilitate significantly the identification of bags and therefore the work of the inspectors, but the lots must in any event be kept separately already by the exporting country.

In the present case of imports to Portugal it is highly recommended to try to find out the real number of bags imported and also the number of bags and the respective lots sold to the agricultural co-operatives.

As a third vessel is still expected for the next weeks, it should be taken into account, to carry out an inspection at the arrival of it. If it shown, that the lots are not loaded separately, a refusal of the consignment is recommended. Only such a stringent measure taken already at the beginning of the chain of trade can force the exporter to follow the prescriptions precisely.

It is obvious, that the loading and shipment in Canada are the bottlenecks of the whole procedure. Therefore, future inspections should be carried out with priority on these aspects. With a second priority, the unloading procedure in the relevant Member State should be another key point for inspections.
A suggested solution could be the shipment of each separated lot in a separate container. 3
Training of laboratory staff involved in the analysis of the bacterial diseases potato ring rot and potato brown rot.
Continue with the plans to re-construct the glasshouses in Haniska, which could solve the potential problems caused by the decentralisation.

Continue with the project to introduce a computerised network between different locations. (4) Improving the reporting and archiving system. (5) Establish the system during the coming vegetation. If necessary and requested, a follow-up inspection, e.g. in one year should be taken into account. 3

It is recommended that the measures already initiated by the European Commission against France for not having transposed the requirements of the last modification (Directive 95/29/EC) of Directive 91/628/EEC (see point 5.8.2) be pursued. Certain non-compliances in the application of Directive 91/628/EEC should be included in such a procedure.
France has to take action to ensure compliance with all parts of Directive 91/628/EEC throughout the whole country until 31.12.1998.

The competent Polish authorities at places of departure should ensure that route plans for horses travelling by road and rail from the interior of Poland towards the South of France, foresee unloading and a 24-hour rest period on their long way. The competent German or French authorities on the way should enforce this (e.g. at Lauterbourg, France, actually a transfer point, that should then be upgraded to a staging point).

The competent German, Dutch and French authorities at places of departure should ensure that route plans for cattle travelling by road and sea to North African countries, foresee unloading and a 24-hour rest period at the transfer points (French Mediterranean ports). The competent French authorities at the ports should enforce this.

It is recommended to invite representatives of Member States to the services of the Commission to discuss how progress could be achieved to improve cooperation between Member States in the field of long-distance transports of animals, in particular with regard to the length of transport aboard ferry boats, to the requirements for loading densities during combined road-and-ferry journeys and to the necessity to exclude animals in advanced pregnancy from being transported.

It is recommended to modify EC legislation in the following areas: · new forms for route plans should be elaborated, · a more precise definition for animals in advanced pregnancy (see point 5.6) should be formulated.

The Greek authorities should implement measures to enhance the awareness of (small) producers on the risks of the presence of harmful organisms in their crops.
The Greek authorities should also implement measures to enhance the awareness of (small) producers on the requirements for protected zones in Greece. 4

Legislation introducing a complete feed ban on MMBM for all livestock species should be implemented.16

The complete feed ban may be reconsidered in view of the implementation of the following conditions: · An effort to trace all the amounts of incompletely treated MMBM including feedstuff in which such MMBM is present or may be present by cross contamination should be made. This material should not be used in the feed chain. The Portuguese authorities should be required therefore to provide figures on the stocks still existing of incompletely processed MMBM, feedstuff batches in which such MMBM may be present, and MMBM and feed containing MMBM produced with SRMs and the measures taken to avoid their use in the feed chain.17 · Measures to dispose of dead ruminants and SRMs should be implemented. · Active collaboration from practitioners is required to increase the feed ban awareness. Any breach of the feedban should be actively followed-up by the Veterinary authorities and effective dissuasive measures should be put in place. · The central veterinary authorities should redirect the BSE surveillance in view of the performances of the local veterinary authorities. The epidemiological information collected at field level on BSE cases should include more detailed information on possible feed-ban breaches and on the origin of all the feedstuff introduced in the farm considering the incubation period of the disease. · The frequency of the official controls should be related to the availability of auditable written procedures in the industry. · Microscopic tests in feedstuff samples should be carried out to ensure the implementation of the MMBM ban. 16 The Portuguese authorities in their comments on the draft provided on 25.9.98, declared that such a measure will be appropriate and will have practical effects if applied to all Member States. 17 According to the Portuguese authorities there are no stocks of MMBM to be reprocessed and legislation to prohibit the use of SRMs in the feed chain has been approved. However in the opinion of the ScVC of 26-27 March 1998, as updated by the Steering Committee of 24-26 September 1998, on saftey of MMBM, it is reported that: "Cannot be excluded that under the worst conditions traces of infectivity could remain (after processing) and in order to minimize a possible remaining risk of infectivity SRMs shall be excluded from the feed chain". As a matter of fact this risk has been reduced only after the implementation of the legal measure announced by the Portuguese authorities and therefore it is not excluded residual exposure by cross contamination or cross feeding. 15
Details on the relations between the positive case discovered by histology and the clinical case should be provided to the Commission. 18

A follow-up mission should be carried out to further verify the control measures to eradicate BSE. 18 According to the Portuguese authorities a report is going to be prepared on this point. 19 The Portuguese authorities in their comments on the draft provided on 25.9.98 declared that the Minister of Agriculture launched an inquiry on this item on 8 September 1998. 20 The Portuguese authorities with their comments on the draft report of 25.9.98 provided an activity program on this point from which inspections to rendering plant processing animal waste other than mammalian has been launched. 16

For the products for which Italy has a protected zone, all producers should be registered, the checks required in Council Directive 77/93/EEC carried out and a plant passport issued when the requirements are met and the products are moved within the protected zone. The Italian authorities are asked to amend the relevant Italian legislation and make the execution coherent with the requirements laid down in Council Directive 77/93/EEC.

Given the serious doubts on its enforcement, and the associated phytosanitary risks, it is suggested to the Italian authorities to reconsider the application of the provisions of local movement. As the provisions are laid down as a "may"-clause in Directive 77/93/EEC, transposition in the Italian legislation is not mandatory. In EC legislation

The Italian authorities are strongly in favour of deletion of the articles in Council Directive 77/93/EEC dealing with local movement and the related items. As a second option mandatory registration and checks can replace the present provisions.
If the provisions are maintained, the Commission should draft clear definitions and monitor its uniform application in the Member States. 5

Resources should be used first of all to improve working conditions in the laboratories and district departments. Every laboratory must have basic equipment. It is absolutely essential to purchase equipment, in particular for laboratories. Where resources are limited, these should be targeted, i.e. a reduction in the number of laboratories should be considered.
Technical training of staff should be carried out only if the laboratories are suitably equipped.
Training in general management/administrative tasks should also be given alongside technical training.
A register of persons and firms subject to phytosanitary instructions is urgently required. This is the only way of guaranteeing that the whole system is monitored by the SPA's inspectors.

Since the majority of border inspection points will no longer be necessary once the Czech Republic becomes a member of the EU, PHARE resources should no longer be used for this purpose, particularly since the border inspection points inspected are operational. 5

It is also recommended that the Czech Republic should make more efficient use of the border inspection points, e.g. by modifying working hours, transferring inspections of exports to district level and abandoning duplicate inspections, carrying out inspections on demand (which is the practice in the Member States) and making inspectors responsible for managing the respective districts.
It is necessary to amend those sections of the legislation relating to the fitting out of border inspection points, in particular with laboratories. 6

Recommendations for the Greek Competent Authorities concerning the eradication programme for the next year · A new control/eradication programme should be elaborated. This programme should begin only when agreement has been achieved relating to the availability of finance, personnel, laboratory capacities, vaccines and an efficient movement control system. This programme should be drafted in agreement with the health authorities and the farmer associations. · In selected areas preliminary field trials on the conjunctival method should be conducted in adult sheep and goats and the results should carefully be evaluated before a mass vaccination programme can be launched. · An immediate public health warning should be instituted to advise the Greeks and tourists on the risks and hazards related to Brucella melitensis infection, especially in relation to cheese produced on the farms on a small scale.

Recommendations for the European Commission · The Payment which has taken place for the 1997 Ovine and Caprine Brucellosis Eradication Programme in Greece should be reconsidered. · Ewe premia and future financial support for the transportation of sheep and goats intended for transhumance should only be given to owners whose flocks are engaged in the Control and Eradication Programme. · An inquiry should be pursued to eliminate the possibility of double financing of the Greek Brucellosis Eradication Programme under veterinary and structural funds having taken place in the years 1992 to 1995. · The opinion of the Scientific Veterinary Committee should be requested concerning - the advantages, in terms of public health protection, of mass vaccination of adult sheep and goats. - the value of the serological tests actually employed in the eradication of Brucella melitensis in sheep and goats. 9

Recommendations for the Commission services : Having verified that the veterinary authorities have acted in a satisfactory way by improving the four establishments to the required standard, and that action is taken to suspend the approval of the fifth establishment, consideration should be given to suspending the infringement proceedings opened by Commission (reference A/96/2022) against France while waiting for further guarantees from the French authorities.

In view of the prevalence of the disease in wild boar and of the speed with which it can move, largely through the activities of hunters, both within national boundaries and across them, veterinary authorities, even those whose area of responsibility contains only a small population of wild boar, must have in place measures which enable them to identify and deal with any evidence of classical swine fever.

In the context of the fight against swine fever it is not possible to operate effectively with control measures which are activated only at the moment when an outbreak is first identified; they must be in place, with the same level of detail and effectiveness, whether the disease is present or not. 7.2. Recommendations to the German authorities 7.2.1. The mission team recommends, in respect at least of the State of North Rhine-Westphalia, the following: · improvements in the cleaning and disinfection of vehicles used for the transport of pigs; · measures to bring about increased official supervision of pig collection centres; · improved supervision of herd registers; · changes in the procedures in semen collection centres to remove the risk of the dissemination of swine fever virus in semen or by any of the activities concerned in the provision of an artificial insemination service. 7.2.2. The German authorities should provide details of the action taken to implement these recommendations by 31 December 1998 (and notify the Food and Veterinary Office thereof). 7.3. Recommendations to the Commission 7.3.1. Increasing specialisation in agriculture has led to whole areas of Europe being devoted to the same aspect of pig production, with the result that pigs have to be transported in large numbers and often over long distances 9 to provide inputs or to reach markets. The mission team recommends that the Commission consider the possibility of a decision requiring that a period of at least thirty days should separate the introduction of pigs to, and any movement of pigs from, a holding, except for pigs sent for direct slaughter. 7.3.2. The introduction of a policy designed to emphasise regional self- sufficiency is also recommended as it would certainly have as a consequence a reduction in the incidence of classical swine fever and, possibly, of other List A diseases. 10

Recommendations to the Dutch authorities 6.1.1. to increase the number of official veterinarians in the slaughterhouses to reach the permanent presence in accordance with article 9 of Directive 64/433/EEC as already recommended in the report on the veterinary mission to the Netherlands of 11 to 15 May 1998 (Doc XXIV/1399/98/final) 6.1.2. to introduce records for animal treatments on farms as quickly as possible 6.1.3. to issue detailed procedures for the official sampling by the end of March 1999 and inform the Commission hereof 6.1.4. to inform the Commission of the new structure of veterinary services as soon as plans are available 6.1.5. to include in such plans adequate training measures for inspectors charged with the sampling to guarantee a sampling strategy as laid down in Commission Decision 98/179/EC 6.1.6. to pursue the development of analytical methods for the detection of substances in the new product groups 6.1.7. to reconsider in the 1999 monitoring plan that the detection limits and levels of action for the examinations of Group A substances should be equal 6.1.8. to divide the responsibilities of the National Reference Laboratories for the specific substance groups before the 1 January 2001 6.1.9. to consider the assignment of the tasks of drawing up the monitoring plan, co-ordination of inspections, data collection and reporting to the Commission to one public body as required by article 4 of Council Directive 96/23/EC 12 of 13 RESIDUES ­ THE NETHERLANDS ­ OCT 98

To the European Commission: 8.2.1 The Scientific Veterinary Committee should examine all relevant data in relation to the immuno-blotting test for the diagnosis of C.B.P.P. with a view to establishing harmonised protocols for the inclusion of this test in E.U. law. 12 8.2.2 The eradication programme should be financed for 1999 in order to eradicate the disease from the remaining areas of Portugal. 13

To the Italian veterinary authorities: The mission team recommends: 6.1.1. that consideration be given to the implications of legal procedures which may result in delays in the destruction of animals involved in an outbreak of a List A disease; 6.1.2. that measures be put in place in Italy to ensure the effective cleaning and disinfection of empty transport vehicles travelling between the non-accredited and the accredited zones in connection with the purchase of accredited breeding stock.

To the veterinary authorities of the Region of Lombardy: The mission team recommends: 6.2.1. that the epidemiological enquiry be continued with all necessary intensity until a positive source of the original infection is identified. In particular, further investigations are required in farms related by ownership to the primary outbreak holding in order to eliminate any possible epidemiological links; 6.2.2. that, where the stamping out of a List A disease is concerned, sufficient resources are allocated to ensure that the epidemiological enquiries are carried out with the greatest possible expedition; 6.2.3. that, in all cases where preventative slaughter is carried out, samples for epidemiological investigation should always be collected. 10

To the Commission services: The mission team recommends: 6.3.1. that a follow-up mission be sent to evaluate in detail the Italian national programme for the eradication of swine vesicular disease; 6.3.2. that the Commission services study as a matter of urgency all aspects of cleaning and disinfection of transport vehicles with a view to issuing guidelines with European Union-wide application; 6.3.3. that the Commission services consider the possibility of a decision requiring that a period of at least thirty days should separate the introduction of pigs to, and any movement of pigs from, a holding. 11

RECOMMENDATIONS TO THE LUXEMBOURG AUTHORITIES Unless another deadline is indicated, the Luxembourg authorities are required to inform the Commission Services of the action taken or planned to address the following recommendations within 25 working days after receiving this report. It is recommended that the CA · provides detailed and comprehensive updated figures on the annual production of feeds and trade in feeds and PAP used for animal consumption, in particular trade in feeds containing processed mammalian waste. · provides detailed information on the controls carried out at farm level. 10 · ensures that traders of PAP like fishmeal used for the production of feeds are aware of the requirements of Article 2 (1) of Commission 97/735/EC and take the necessary action towards implementation. · checks for the documentation as required by Article 4 (1) of Council Directive 92/118/EEC referring to Annex I Chapter 4. during control visits to traders of petfood in those cases where the feeds are directly traded from manufacturers into Luxembourg and inform the traders about these legal requirements. · adopts instructions to ensure that carcasses and the internal organs of positive bovines are destroyed in accordance with Article 4 of Decision 97/534/EC as foreseen by Article 3 (2) of Commission Decision 98/272/EC. · focusses on sampling moribund cattle as foreseen by Commission Decision 98/272/EC rather than taking samples from slaughter cows fit for human consumption where the number of available bovines with neurological symptoms does not meet the defined target number.

NATIONAL RULES FOR SPECIFIED RISK MATERIAL Commission Decision 97/534/EC entered into force in Luxembourg as a national initiative. As no Community legislation on SRM is yet in place it is proposed that the CA ensures that the competent authority at the place of destination is informed whenever material defined as SRM is traded. This information is essential to enable the competent authority at the place of destination to apply any national rules for SRM.

RECOMMENDATION TO THE COMMISSION It is recommended to clarify whether the provisions laid down in Annex I and II to Commission Decision 97/735/EC are applicable to trade in feeds containing processed mammalian animal protein. 11

Recommendations to the Irish authorities: - The Department of the Marine and Natural Resources, as the national competent authority should be given the legal powers to close down the production areas. - The supervision of the establishments should put more emphasis on documentary checks. In particular, attention should be given so that registration documents and ledger books are used according to their purpose. - Better formalisation of the classification procedures and of the design of monitoring programmes, specifically by making available written protocols, defined sampling points and procedures, would consolidate the system in place. - Shellfish should not be dispatched without being packed and labelled according to the Directive requirements, even when placed on the local market. - In the establishment concerned the microbiological analysis of final product should be organised so that the establishment will be provided with the results on a regular basis, ensuring a permanent control of the quality of the shellfish by the establishment itself. - Frequency of the inspections should be at such a level as to ensure full compliance of the establishments with the Directive.

Recommendations to the European Commission: - Further clarification is needed regarding the use, purpose and design of the registration document. - A working group should be established to update Directive 91/492/EEC. Microbiological and phytotoxicity aspects would have in particular to be considered, in order to better protect public health. The Irish authorities specifically asked the Commission to organise a working group. - DSP and biotoxin intercalibration test should be organised soon to ensure the same level of safety of the shellfish produced in the Member States. 6

MISSION DETAILS The mission took place from 6 ­ 10 September 1999. 1.1. Mission team The mission team consisted of 3 veterinary inspectors from the FVO, Unit 1. 2 representatives from the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia ­ VARS (Central Competent Authority - CCA) accompanied the inspection team throughout the mission. 1.2. Sites visited Two approved slaughterhouses / cutting plants were visited, one of which also had a meat products section (not approved). An unapproved integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment was visited at the request of the Slovenian authorities who adjudged that the establishment was in compliance with EC requirements1. An approved meat products establishment and an approved wild game processing establishment were also visited. An initial meeting and a final meeting took place in the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia in Ljubljana.

OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The scope of the mission was indicated in an official letter from the Director of the FVO to the relevant authorities in Slovenia: the issues to be addressed during the mission were the controls on the production of fresh meat, meat products and game meat for export to the European Community. As part of the above, the team also assessed animal identification and traceability systems as required by Council Directives 72/462/EEC and 96/23/EC. In carrying out its mission, the team focussed on the structure and performance of the veterinary authorities in ensuring that the provisions of Community law are respected in relation to exports of fresh meat, game meat and meat products to the Community. In particular, compliance with the provisions of the following Community legislation was assessed: Council Directive 72/462/EEC (as amended) of 12 December 1972 on health and veterinary inspection problems upon importation of bovine, ovine and caprine animals and swine, fresh meat or meat products from third countries. 1 The Slovenian authorities have commented on this point. No changes have been made to the original text. Page 3 of 16 Council Directive 92/45/EEC of 16 June 1992 on public health and animal health problems relating to the killing of wild game and the placing on the market of wild- game meat. Council Directive 92/118/EEC of 17 December 1992 laying down animal health and public health requirements governing trade in and imports into the Community of products not subject to the said requirements laid down in specific Community rules referred to in Annex A (I) to Directive 89/662/EEC and, as regards pathogens, to Directive 90/425/ EEC. The following additional aspects were also assessed: Requirements relating to the traceability of animals contained in Council Directive 96/23/EC of 29 April 1996 on measures to monitor certain substances and residues thereof in live animals and animal products. Certification of wild game meat (Commission Decision 97/218/EC). Certification of farmed game meat (Commission Decision 97/219/EC).

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation governing the performance of on-the-spot checks in third countries and in particular: Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries and Commission Decision 86/474/EEC of 11 September 1986 on the implementation of the on-the-spot inspections to be carried out in respect of the importation of bovine animals and swine and fresh meat from non-member countries Council Decision 95/408/EC of 22 June 1995 on the conditions for drawing up, for an interim period, provisional lists of third country establishments from which Member States are authorised to import certain products of animal origin, fishery products or live bivalve molluscs.

text: BACKGROUND This mission was part of a series of missions to Eastern European applicant States provided for in the mission programme of the FVO (DG SANCO) and covering the same issues. Various public health (fresh meat) missions have been carried out in Slovenia in the past, the most recent having been undertaken in 1998 (Document XXIV/1390/98). The report of this mission made recommendations with regard to: · Improvement of the documentation relating to veterinary supervision of establishments. Page 4 of 16 · Definition, improvement and enforcement of the approval procedures for establishments. · Reassessment of the layout, maintenance and cleanliness of meat products establishments. · Improvement in the hygiene of operations and the associated technical equipment. · Improvement of the operation and documentation of establishment own check systems. · Approval of establishment own check systems by the competent authority.

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Structure of the Competent Authority The competent authority comprises two component organisations ­ the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia (VARS) and the Animal Health Centre (AHC). The Central Competent Authority in Slovenia is the (VARS) which forms part of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food. The structure and responsibilities of the VARS are outlined below. It should be noted that the VARS is not responsible for the provision of day to day supervision in establishments (see section 5.1.2. below)2. 5.1.1. Structure and responsibilities of the VARS The central office of the VARS is based in Ljubljana under the responsibility of the Chief Veterinary Officer. The VARS has 12 regional offices. The central office of the VARS is responsible for the following: · Policy in the veterinary field. · Drafting and proposing legislation in the veterinary field; · Approval of establishments for the Slovenian market; · Proposing (to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food) the approval of establishments for export markets (including the EC market); · Control of imports of products of animal origin. This includes the issuing of specific import licenses for such products and direct responsibility for Border Inspection Posts. · Drafting and approval of veterinary export certificates. 2 In their commentary on the draft report, the Slovenian authorities have stressed that the VARS does not have the power to appoint Official Veterinarians. They further state that the Slovenian system for authorisation of Official Veterinarians is contrary to European law ­ this appears to be a misunderstanding of EC law and the mission team made no such assertion. Page 5 of 16 · Scrutiny of and suggestion of amendments to the annual implementation plan of the Animal Health Centre (AHC ­ see below for the structure and responsibilities of the AHC). VARS does not have the power to insist on changes to the AHC plan. Authority for approval of the plan rests with the Minister and the Government. · Organising and delivery of training of VARS staff (a number of workshops are held in conjunction with the AHC). The regional offices of the VARS are responsible for the following · Monitoring of the approval conditions is establishments. This is carried out by regional inspectors of the VARS on a regular basis (monitoring visits in the past were carried out monthly, however this is being amended to an inspection every two months). · The taking of appropriate action where establishments are found not to be in compliance with requirements. Such action may include suspension of export certification, reduction of the rate of production or interruption of the production process until the deficiencies detected are rectified. The regional inspectors of the VARS may propose, to the Minister via the central office, the suspension or revocation of the approval of an establishment. · Initial stages of the establishment approval process (see below). Neither the central nor the regional offices of the VARS have the powers to directly control the implementation of veterinary legislation by the AHC. 5.1.2. Structure and responsibilities of the AHC: The AHC was established as an independent body by the Government of Slovenia. The AHC has a central office based in Ljubljana and is made up of nine organisational units. The AHC is responsible for the day to day delivery of veterinary services throughout Slovenia, including the supervision of the production of fresh meat, game meat and meat products. Other sections of the AHC provide, inter alia, disease control and laboratory diagnostic services. AHC staff have the power to control or stop production. They may also report deficiencies to the regional VARS inspector so that appropriate action may be taken at that level. 5.2. Controls in establishments In relation to controls in establishments, the mission team focused on approval of establishments, veterinary supervision (including traceability and certification of meat and meat products and establishments' own checks), supervision by the regional veterinary authorities and slaughter hygiene. Page 6 of 16 5.2.1. Approval of establishments The system in place until this year may be summarised as follows: · Establishments are required to apply to the local municipality for approval to erect a factory or to modify an existing establishment (this is a general requirement which applies to all types of enterprise and not merely to food producing establishments). The application must be accompanied by detailed plans. · The municipality circulates the plans to the relevant authorities (environment, medical, etc.). In the case of the veterinary authorities, the regional office of the VARS was required to comment on and approve plans ­ conditional approval could be given subject to stated modifications to the plans being made. · Having received the comments of all the authorities consulted, the municipality grants approval for building to commence. The comments received are attached to the approval documentation. Where conditions have been set by any of the authorities consulted these should be incorporated into the plans. · When building is completed, the relevant authorities (including the regional VARS office) are asked to visit the premises and confirm that the building is in compliance with the plans approved, including any modifications stipulated. · At this stage, the operator may apply for temporary approval pending a final decision. · Assuming the building has been deemed to be satisfactory, the regional VARS office informs the central VARS office and national approval is granted. · At this time the operator may apply to the regional AHC for the provision of an inspection service. · Should the operator wish to gain approval for export, he is required to apply to VARS. Following a satisfactory VARS inspection, export approval is proposed to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food who may then grant such approval. Earlier in 1999, VARS introduced a revised system for the inspection of establishments prior to approval whereby this is undertaken by a team of three experts appointed from a central list of such persons however this system was not in place in relation to any of the establishments visited during the mission. Page 7 of 16 Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 13 During an FVO mission to Slovenia in 1998, the mission team found that an integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment (all parts approved for export to EC) and a separate meat products and meat preparations establishment (approved for export of meat products to EC) shared the same approval number (both establishments were owned by the same company). The separate meat products establishment was found not to be in compliance with Community requirements and, as a consequence, the Slovenian authorities were requested to delete the separate meat products establishment and the products section of the integrated establishment from the EC approval list. This was done. Subsequently the Slovenian authorities re-approved, for export to the EC, a section of the detached meat products establishment and assigned a new approval number to this part of the establishment. The products section of the integrated establishment remained unapproved for export to the EC. The procedures for approval of establishments, as outlined above, were not followed in the case and no documentation relating to the process was available. This year the mission team re-visited both the integrated and the detached establishments. In relation to the integrated establishment the mission team was asked to assess the products section to determine whether it could be recommended for approval for export to the EC. In relation to the detached establishment, the mission team was asked to confirm approval for that section to which the Slovenian authorities had granted approval for the export of meat products to the EC. The mission team discovered that the unapproved section of the detached establishment continued to be approved for the Slovenian market with its old approval number which was the same as that used by the integrated establishment for which meat products approval was being sought. Prior to the inspection of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment, the mission team was assured by the Slovenian authorities that this section of the establishment had been completely segregated from other, unapproved parts of the establishment and a plan of the establishment was shown to illustrate this. This assurance was found to be false ­ two rooms for storage and weighing/mixing of spices for an unapproved meat products section were discovered within the approved section (the door from the intake area of the approved section to these rooms was not shown on the plan; the mission team were assured, prior to the door being opened, that the door was permanently locked, however, the rooms were in constant use and the only access to them was via the approved section of the establishment); It was also discovered that part of the EC 3 The Slovenian commentary on the draft report states that the establishment was ordered to ensure complete physical separation between the EC approved and non-EC approved sections of the establishment. It is clear from the commentary that approval was subsequently granted without the performance of any verification that this order had been followed. No changes to the text have been made. Page 8 of 16 approved meat products establishment was utilised for the production of raw meat preparations for the local market ­ production of raw meat preparations took place in an area adjacent to the area used for wrapping and packaging of cooked meat products. The mission team also found a new door between the approved section and the unapproved section (where cooked sausages were produced for the local market); raw carton packed meat and cooked sausages were found behind this door proving that it was in regular use and that the EC approved section of the establishment was not adequately separated from the sausage section. The layout of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment was not in compliance with EC requirements: there was no logical product flow with many cross-overs of cooked and raw meat and packaged and exposed meat and meat products; routes for evacuation of soiled cardboard were not acceptable. Approval of the meat products section of the integrated slaughter establishment would have led to a situation where it shared an approval number with an unapproved meat products and thus given rise to the potential for fraudulent exports of meat products from the non-approved establishment to the EC. Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 2 The team also visited an unapproved integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment which was at an advanced stage of the approval process. The Slovenian authorities adjudged the establishment to be in compliance with EC requirements and they wanted to add it to the list of approved export establishments. The construction of the meat products section of this establishment had completed in late 1998. While some of the initial aspects of the approval procedure described above had been followed, the process had not been completed and, in any case, was demonstrably ineffective. Documentation was available which showed that plans had been submitted to the municipality prior to commencement of the project and that these plans had been examined by a regional VARS veterinarian who had approved the plans providing four stipulated alterations were made. Approval for building to commence had been issued by the municipality. Building work had been completed in November 1998 and production commenced at that time however the municipality had not issued a request for an inspection to verify that the establishment had been constructed in accordance with the plans received until mid 1999 and this inspection had not been completed at the time of the FVO visit even though, by that time, the establishment had been in production for approximately 10 months. Documentation was available which showed that the establishment had applied to the regional AHC office for the provision of an inspection service. This request had been complied with by the AHC. Documentation was available which showed that a provisional approval, valid until the end of 1998 had been granted by the VARS. No documentation illustrating the basis on which this decision had been taken was available. Page 9 of 16 No documentation extending this provisional approval was available and the establishment was, therefore, operating in contravention of Slovenian regulations. The plans approved contained many deficiencies in layout with many cross- flows with the potential to cause hygiene problems. One very serious deficiency entailed raw meat being prepared beside the cooker doors. Cooked meat was removed form the cookers by the operatives who handled raw meat. Cooked meat emerging from the cookers comes into close proximity with raw meat. These processes, therefore, constitute a serious public health risk. Only two of the conditions imposed by the regional VARS had been complied with however it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. The building had not been constructed in accordance with the plans submitted ­ again it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. 5.2.2. Official Veterinary supervision in establishments: The numbers of veterinarians assigned to establishments were satisfactory in all cases. However, as detailed below, the effectiveness of veterinary supervision was unsatisfactory in virtually all establishments visited. On a number of occasions during the mission, the mission team was given information which subsequently was found to be false (e.g. in one establishment the team were told that a locked room was empty when it, in fact, contained ingredients, packaging material and building materials). Training of Official Veterinarians : The VARS has established a training programme for its staff. AHC personnel receive some training from the VARS. The AHC does not have a training programme for the official veterinarians. Documentation containing instructions for the official veterinarians has been issued by the VARS over a number of years. This documentation is quite comprehensive, however, many of the official veterinarians in the establishments appeared to be unaware of the existence of part or all of these instructions. In relation to many of the aspects of supervision detailed below, the official veterinarians did not appear to understand their significance or the underlying principles. Water quality: · Plans of the water distribution systems were not always up-to-date. · All establishments had good systems for the rotation of water sampling points. · In one establishment, the regional AHC laboratory had unilaterally reduced the range of tests carried out on water samples. This problem had not Page 10 of 16 been identified by the official veterinarian or by the regional VARS inspector. Medical certification of workers: · A comprehensive system for medical examination and certification of workers was in place throughout Slovenia. · Checking of the operation of this system (by both the establishment and the official veterinarian) was insufficient in all establishments visited ­ many documents were not signed and/or dated. Scrutiny of establishments'own check programmes: · A major effort was in progress to introduce own check systems in meat product establishments with application of HACCP principles. The legal basis requiring the development of own checks is not yet in place however this is scheduled for September 1999. · In some establishments, the official veterinarian was involved in the development of own check systems, however, the own checks systems were not always comprehensive. · In one establishment it was found that the annual programme of the AHC was not being respected in that the programme specified that 40 bacteriological samples per month should be taken by the official veterinarian and analysed by the official service (AHC). The official veterinarian collected 40 samples per month, however, only 10 of these were analysed by the AHC laboratory ­ the remaining samples were analysed in the establishment's own laboratory. No differentiation was made between establishment results and AHC results and it was therefore not possible for the official veterinarian to verify the accuracy of the establishment sampling programme. Pest control: · Pest control programmes were in place in all establishments, however, these programmes were not sufficiently comprehensive and were not systematically supervised

In relation to animal protection during transport, full harmonisation of the operational conduct between veterinary services is said to be underway including detailed procedures for recording and filing of the data on the checks carried out. With reference to the specific welfare problems in one of the plants visited, the statement specifies that the veterinary service of the establishment took the appropriate measures in respect of the transport company on 8 October 1999 to ensure restoration of the correct transport conditions. In relation to protection of animals at the time of slaughter, the CA stated that they are acquiring further data and information on this subject also with a view to possible assessment and definition by the Scientific Committee of the most appropriate technical features for stunning equipment. With regard to the protection of the laying hens in battery cages, the CA declare that they are now preparing appropriate guidelines with a view to improving the harmonisation of operating procedures throughout the whole country. Immediate extension of surveys outside the current infested zone to high risk pine areas (those in proximity to wood processing facilities) and to wood processing facilities. Sampling at the processing yards should include the wood itself plus chip/bark piles as well as trace- back of sources of wood supplied to the mills. Surveys in the forests should take account of the likelihood that PWN infestation of living trees may not lead to wilt symptoms taking account of the lower average temperatures in more northerly locations. Samples should include recently dead trees, those showing wilt symptoms and, to a lesser extent, live trees.
Systematic surveys of all remaining pine areas using the methods mentioned above.

For the year 2000 flight season, flight traps for the presence of Monochamus spp. should be established in forest locations and at wood processing facilities in both the PWN-infested and currently non-infested areas. The traps should be based on a more open design, such as funnel traps or cross-vane traps, and should include monoterpene attractants (further details about traps and the most suitable attractants should be assessed from the literature). Programme of corrective measures A programme of measures should be developed and implemented to rectify the deficiencies detailed in this report. This programme should be comprehensive and detailed. The programme should be submitted to the European Commission. The programme should include the following: (a) Legislative measures The Veterinary Practice Act should be reconstructed. The roles, responsibilities and powers of the veterinary organisations, particularly the official services, should be defined and collated. Other legislation should be amended to eliminate the deficiencies noted in this report. New legislation should be drafted and introduced where necessary. (b) Training A comprehensive syllabus for training of the staff of the VARS should be developed. The syllabus should cover, at least, the following subjects: Ø The responsibilities of the official veterinarian, Ø Slaughter hygiene techniques, Ø Control of health marks and health marked labels, Ø Traceability of meat, Ø Certification, Ø HACCP and the supervision of establishment "own check" programmes and 15 Ø The layout of establishments and the assessment of blueprints. As part of the training programme, a manual for the use of official veterinarians should be developed. This manual should expand and clarify legislative requirements and should detail the supervisory and enforcement tasks necessary to implement the legislation. The TAIEX organisation and the services of the European Commission should be approached for assistance in the delivery of this training. (c) Veterinary supervision in establishments In addition to the operations manual referred to at 7.1.1(b) above, a series of checklists and schedules should be developed to aid the official veterinarians in their work and to harmonise enforcement activities. As a priority, veterinary certification, the supervision of establishment "own checks" programmes and the control of health marks (particularly health marked labels) should be improved. (d) VARS supervision ­ regional and central Criteria and timetables for the inspection of establishments and supervision of official veterinarians by the regional inspectorate should be developed and implemented. The management role of the regional inspectors should be emphasised and enhanced. The "expert commission" should evaluate establishments and the performance of the regional inspectors and local official veterinarians on behalf of the central office of the VARS. This should be done on a regular, structured basis; however, the frequency of such evaluations should not be excessive and should not undermine the relationship between the regional inspectors and the official veterinarians in the establishments. (e) Approval of establishments A protocol should be developed for use by the "expert commission" when approving establishments or assessing their approval status. A programme for re-assessment of all establishments should be put in place. Deficiencies in existing establishments should be identified and deadlines for rectification agreed with the operators of the establishments concerned. (f) Animal identification and movement controls The programme set out in the legislation should be followed. Safeguards and controls should be incorporated in the database structure and functionality. The on-the-spot checks (e.g. on farm, in market, at slaughter) necessary to ensure the effectiveness of the system should be formulated. Additional legislation should be enacted where necessary. 16

INTRODUCTION The mission took place in Germany from 28 February to 03 March 2000. The mission team comprised two inspectors from the FVO. The mission was undertaken as part of the FVO's planned mission programme. The inspection team was accompanied during the whole mission by at least one representative from the central CAs. An opening meeting was held on 28 February 2000 with the central CAs and representatives of the CA of the Federal States SH and MV at the BMG. At this meeting, the inspection team confirmed the objectives of and itinerary for the mission, and additional information required for the satisfactory completion of the mission was requested. The final meeting was held 3 March 2000 at BgVV with the CA of the Federal States SH and MV and the BgVV (no representatives of the central CAs participated at this meeting).

OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objective of the mission was to carry out an evaluation of the transposition and application of Council Directive 92/46/EEC laying down the health rules for the production and placing on the market of raw milk, heat-treated milk and milk-based products in Germany. In order to assess the performance of the official control services, visits to several establishments, a farm and laboratories chosen by the CAs were carried out. This was the first mission undertaken in Germany for this purpose. It forms part of a 2-year series of similar missions to all Member States. At the end of this programme a summary report will be issued. In pursuit of this objective, the following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Central (BMG) 1 Federal States (Land level) 2 LABORATORY VISITS Central/reference 1 Inter-professional laboratory 1 FOOD PROCESSING ESTABLISHMENTS On-farm production of milk based products 1 Caseinate producing establishment 1 Milk processing establishments 1 LIVE ANIMAL CONTROL SITES Farms 1 6

text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Production and trade information 4.1.1. Milk production in Germany From 1988 to 1997 the number of dairy farms has decreased by 38,2% from 278,300 in 1988 to 172,200 in 1997. Also the number of dairy cows has decreased by 28,1% from 6,992,700 to 5,026,000. However, in the same time period the average production/cow increased by 22,2 % from 4,568 kg to 5,575 kg. Also the average number of cows/dairy farm has increased by 15,9 % from 25,2 to 29,2. In 1999, Germany had a milk quota of 27.8 million tonnes. The central CA (BML) and the CA of SH1 had no separate statistics on the sheep and goat milk production. The main part of this production is used for direct sale or processed further on the farm and sold directly to the consumer. 4.1.2. Dairy industry The production of dairy products in Germany in 1997 is presented in the following table: Product type Amount In % (tonnes) Drinking milk and cream 8165,5 71,2 Condenced milk 566,0 4,9 Butter 442,4 3,9 Cheese 1590,1 13,9 Melted cheese 150,1 1,3 Milk powder 548,0 4,7 Casein/caseinates 10,6 0,09 Total 11.472,7 100 1 See comments of the German CA 7 4.2. Health information 4.2.1. Animal health situation Germany profits from a favourable animal health situation for bovines, sheep and goats: Ø Foot and mouth disease: freedom since 1989 Ø Bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis: Germany is officially free from bovine tuberculosis (Commission Decisions 99/467/EC and 2000/69/EEC) and brucellosis (Commission Decisions 99/466/EC and 2000/69/EEC) and also free from Brucella melitensis (Commission Decision 93/52/EEC). The monitoring of bovine Brucellosis is based on testing of the tank milks every second year with ELISA and of Brucella melitensis on random testing of 5 % of the animals annually. The screening for bovine tuberculosis is based mostly on the post mortem controls. 4.2.2. Food poisonings and zoonoses In 1993-1997, 4,7 % of food poisoning outbreaks were caused by milk and milk products (33/782 outbreaks). Of these outbreaks, 7 were caused by Campylobacter sp.. In 1998, one outbreak (source cheese made from raw milk) was caused by S. aureus. No milk and milk product related data on salmonellosis was available, but the total number of persons with enteritis infections caused by Salmonella serovars in 1999 was 85,015. The number of human brucellosis cases in 1999 was 21, of Q fever 276 and of newborn listeriosis 31 (data published by the federal authority Robert-Koch- Institute). In 1999 there were 2 microbiological alerts for German milk products (both Listeria monocytogenes in cheeses).

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legislation · German national legislation on food hygiene of milk and milk products The basic food hygiene legislation is formed by: Ø LMBG, BGBl. I Nr. 36, p.1169 Framework law on food hygiene with general regulations, orders and prohibitions for protection of the consumers against health dangers and deceptions. Ø Verordnung über Lebensmittelhygiene und zur Änderung der Lebensmitteltransportbehälter-Verordnung (Ordinance on Food hygiene and to Change of the Ordinance of food transport containers, BGBl. I Nr. 56, p. 2008) More specific regulations on food hygiene. Council Directive 92/46/EEC is transposed into German law by: · MVO of 24 April 1995 (BGBl. I Nr. 21 of the 3.5.1995, p. 544) and · MGVO of 9 July 1980 (BGBl. I Nr. 36 of the 12.7.1980, p. 878). 8 · Comparison of the German legislation with the EU legislation The German legislation on milk hygiene differs in some points from Council Directive 92/46/EEC2: 1. Establishments selling heat-treated milk, butter and certain cheeses (Hard, semi-hard and soft cheeses) to retail shops do not need an approval (para 20 point 2 of MVO, mittelbare Abgabe an den Verbraucher). 2. The definition for direct sale includes also selling of products on the local weekly markets (Wochenmärkte). 3. The requirement for the on-the-spot treatment of milk from sheep and goats deriving from holdings not free of Brucella melitensis has not been transcribed. This has however no practical consequences, as Germany is free from the disease. 4. The definition of thermisised milk as far as the duration of the heat treatment is concerned differs from the provisions of Council Directive 92/46/EEC. 5. Germany has included in its legislation the possibility to approve establishments which are not on the list of establishments from which Member States are allowed to import milk and milk products in the approved third countries. However, this possibility is not practised.

Art. 27 of Council Directive 92/46/EEC has not been transcribed into the national milk hygiene legislation. However, BgVV and BafM have been designated as the NRLs and this has also been notified to the Community.
The sanitary register, as required in Directive 96/23/EC, Art. 10, is not completely transposed into the national legislation.
Council Directive 96/43/EC was not yet transcribed in SH (however, the transposition process was on its way and transposition was completed on the 22.3.2000).

The Milk Hygiene Ordinance contains specific rules for manufacturers who sell non-heat-treated raw milk either directly from the farm to the consumer or as certified milk (Vorzugsmilch). At the place for the sale of raw milk it has to be indicated by a sign that the milk should be boiled before consumption. Certified milk undergoes regular bacteriological controls on pathogens and can be put on the market only as packed ready for sale.
In the definition of composite milk products, which cannot otherwise be classified, the product's dry weight components have to consist of at least 50 % of milk and milk based components.

Ice-cream is defined as a milk product, if it contains milk and milk-based products, irrespective of their amounts. 2 See comments of the German CA 9 5.2. Competent Authority 5.2.1. General structure of the German CA At the federal level, the veterinary services responsible for the co-ordination of all the activities concerning the policy and the implementation of Council Directive 92/46/EEC fall under the responsibility of 2 Ministries, BMG and BML. BMG is in general responsible for the transposition of the Directive 92/46/EEC and has issued the primary legislation for this purpose. BML is responsible for the transposition of the legislation concerning raw milk quality control and has issued primary legislation for this purpose. The application of Council Directive 92/46/EEC is under the responsibility of the Federal States (Länder) (total number 16), each of which has its own Government (Landesregierung). The local CAs are formed by the Districts (Kreise). The total number of Kreises in Germany is 439. In some Federal States an intermediate level, "Bezirksregierung or Regierungspräsidium", exists between the Federal State and the Kreis level (total number 32). The SVUs (total number 36), operating under the supervision of the Federal States, form a part of the veterinary administration. Ø Audits In none of the CA levels visited, were systems of audits applied in the field of milk hygiene. 5.2.2. Central level Ø BMG The BMG and its Directorate of Veterinary Medicine, Division 422 (Foodstuff of Animal Origin) is responsible for the co-ordination of all the activities concerning the policy and the implementation for Directive 92/46/EEC. Within BMG 4 veterinary officers work in Division 422, of whom 1.5 work mostly with milk hygiene matters. Division 422 is also responsible for the co-ordination of the Rapid Alert System and receives and transmits the messages between the Commission and the responsible CA in the Federal State. Responsibilities for the official control of drinking water and of residue monitoring are in the same Ministry but fall under the responsibility of other Divisions. Ø BML The BML and its Directorate Market Policy, Division 423 (General and special aspects of the milk market) is, inter alia, responsible for legislative activities on the raw milk quality at the farm level. The number of staff working within the unit for milk market is 7, of which 1 deals half-time with raw milk quality aspects. The BML maintains the Federal Dairy Research Centre in Kiel, which also functions as a NRL for milk and milk products (see 5.4.2). 10 Ø BgVV Ø General description of responsibilities BgVV is a scientifically orientated and independent superior federal authority with both administrative and scientific tasks. It is responsible to the BMG. Ø Special tasks related to Directive 92/46/EEC The BgVV is responsible for the official compilation of procedures for sampling and testing foods and additives (Amtliche Sammlung von Untersuchungsverfahren according to para 35 of LMBG). The official published compilation was available. The procedures are defined through co-operation between experts from the food control authorities, consumers, science and the industry concerned. Within BgVV one veterinary officer is working with the aspects of milk hygiene. BgVV has been named as the NRL for milk and milk products (see 5.4.2.). Ø Training and publications BgVV organises annually 2 one-day seminars for the veterinary officers and other staff working in the field of food hygiene. For 2000 one seminar is planned on salmonellosis, the other on safety of foodstuffs.3 BgVV has launched several milk hygiene-related publications/press releases in the recent years, which the mission team received. 5.2.3. It formed part of a wider series of missions to all Member States evaluating control systems and operational standards in this sector. /(*$/ %$6( The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Council Directive 80/217/EEC1 of 22 January 1980 introducing Community measures for the control of classical swine fever. 1 Official Journal L 047, 21/02/1980 p. 0011 - 0023 4 · Council Directive 90/423/EEC2 of 26 June 1990 amending Directive 85/511/EEC3 of 18 November 1985, introducing Community measures for the control of FMD. · Commission Decision 91/42/EEC4 of 8 January 1991 laying down the criteria to be applied when drawing up contingency plans for the control of FMD, in application of Article 5 of Council Directive 90/423/EEC5. · Commission Decision 98/139/EC6 of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in Member States. %$&.*5281' +LVWRU\ The FMD and CSF non-vaccination policy adopted by the EU together with increasing trade, reduction in border controls and the illegal movements of animals have increased the risks of an outbreak and have highlighted the importance of developing suitable contingency plans. As a consequence, Community legislation requirements have been put in place and each Member State is required to draw up a contingency plan and a manual of operations for the two diseases. Between 1973 and 1975 a number of outbreaks of FMD were recorded in Austria; the isolates were of type O and C. The last two outbreaks were declared in 1981 in Lower Austria. The first involved a herd of five pigs and the second a herd with 37 cattle. The virus isolated in the two outbreaks was type O. The source was not identified but an illegal import or swill feeding were suspected. CSF was first reported in Austria in 1921. A number of outbreaks were recorded between 1990 and 1994 and one in 1995 in Lower Austria in a large modern farm, not involved in swill feeding or import. Recommendations to the Member State 10.2.1. Disease control measures A number of improvements or corrective actions need to be taken without any delay in order to increase the efficacy of the disease control measures and, thus, considerably decrease the risk of further spread. The Italian authorities should inform the Commission, within 5 days of receipt of the draft of this report, of the action taken in this respect. (1) Italy should put a stronger emphasis on thorough epidemiological inquiries. For this purpose, the relevant epidemiological units should be reinforced (with human and other resources). Intensive contacts between the different units should be developed or, even better, a single unit should be created in view of the multiple contacts between the two regions. The epidemiologists need to have access to all relevant information without delay and report clearly back to the authorities with possible recommendations for measures to be taken. (2) The Italian authorities should carry out preventive slaughter of poultry flocks, which as a result of the epidemiological inquiries or in view of their location, are clearly at risk of infection. (3) Permanent contact between the affected contiguous regions involved should be reinforced or, where necessary, put in place. Clear information on the results of such contacts should be available. 19 Mission report Italy - avian influenza (03 - 05.01.2000) DG(SANCO)/1112/2000-MR FINAL (4) The control measures in the different controlled zones should be reinforced. For this purpose, clear information to the public should be in place to indicate the borders of the different zones. The veterinary authorities should have close collaboration with enforcement authorities such as the "carabinieri" and the municipal police in order to increase the level and quality of surveillance and install road blocks or other means for enforcement of movement bans. (5) Intensive contacts with farmers and their organisations should be organised in order to increase their awareness of the seriousness of the situation and to improve their knowledge of the applicable control measures. As far as possible, press releases should be complemented with on-the-spot information meetings.

The organisation and functioning of the crisis centres at different levels should be more clearly specified. 10.2.2. Reporting and notification The notification of outbreaks to the Commission and the other Member States, as well as the reporting in general, need to be improved without any delay in order to decrease the risk of any spread to other countries and to allow the relevant authorities to decide whether additional safeguard measures are needed. The Italian authorities should inform the Commission, within 5 days of receipt of the draft of this report, of the action taken in this respect. (1) Italy should endeavour to centralise all information on the outbreaks in the different regions, and to constitute a list with a national numbering system. (2) The Italian CCA should follow the ADNS system (codes) in accordance with Council Directive 82/894/EEC for reporting outbreaks to the Commission and the other Member States, even when not all numerical details are completely available at the time of reporting. 10.2.3. Contingency plan In order to have a full implementation of Council Directive 92/40/EEC, Italy should, within 3 months of the receipt of the final version of this report, submit its draft contingency plan for avian influenza to the Commission, in accordance with Article 17, Paragraph 3 of this Directive. 20 Mission report Italy - avian influenza (03 - 05.01.2000) DG(SANCO)/1112/2000-MR FINAL ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)1112/2000 Competent Authority's (CA) response to the recommendations in the report In their fax of 1 March 2000, the CA has not given any indication of action taken in response to the recommendations in the report. 21

They claim to have suffered damages following the vaccination of their herds and to present their case, they created a foundation (SIS) which subsequently filed a claim for compensation against the vaccine producer for allegedly selling contaminated IBR vaccine. The claim is based on an inventory collated by SIS of the damages incurred by the industry.1 Conclusive links between these health problems and the vaccine have, however, not been established. The position of the CA so far, has been that these reports do not refer to a specific health problem, but primarily to socio-economic difficulties suffered by the farmers concerned and as such, the Dutch government has no direct involvement. The Commission services were informed by the Dutch authorities at an early stage of the existence of a contaminated batch of live attenuated vaccine for IBR and the consequences observed in treated animals. At a later stage, as press releases and parliamentary questions drew attention to the appearance of apparently high numbers of cattle in the Netherlands with a wasting condition, the Commission Services made a request to the MLNV for further clarification of the actual situation. Information was collected during interviews with the Dutch CA in relation to the development of this problem and the action they had taken. This is summarised below, and reflects information provided by these authorities during earlier communications with the Commission services. ­ The control of IBR started in 1998 in the Netherlands requiring the compulsory vaccination of all cattle, except for animals in officially IBR free herds. Both live and inactivated marker vaccines were available. In February 1999, after vaccination with live vaccine, severe symptoms of disease (leading to death in many instances) were recorded on 12 farms, one of them comprising separate production units. One batch of IBR vaccine was found to be contaminated with a virulent type of BVD virus (type 2). All cattle on these 12 farms, approximately 1400 animals, were slaughtered and destroyed. In order to obtain a better picture of the possible side effects of the vaccines, a record (the CA refers to an "inventory") was made of the symptoms observed after the IBR vaccination up to June 1999. Some of the symptoms reported related to cattle with a wasting condition (approximately 350 farms). These are cows in milk which over a period of time become emaciated. It is not clear whether or not these symptoms are connected to vaccination with IBR vaccines. Generally the condition of these animals improves if they are dried off. Tests have not yet revealed the presence of infectious agents. Every effort is being made to find the cause of the problem and in addition to tests on the affected animals, farm management is being looked into (high production holdings) as is the relation between the symptoms and the vaccine. Metabolic causes such as mineral deficiency are also being considered. 1 $ VXEVHTXHQW VWXG\ LGHQWLILHG IDUPV ZKHUH ORQJWHUP SUREOHPV ZHUH UHSRUWHG 12/07/00 - 38579 A number of animals appear to have shortages of cobalt/vitamin B12 and improve considerably when cobalt/vitamin B12 is administered. ­ The farms affected are being visited by the National Inspection Service for Livestock and Meat (RVV), an implementing body of the MLNV, and the Inspectorate for Health Protection, Commodities and Veterinary Public Health (IW&V) of the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (MVWS). If necessary the animals and/or products on these farms are declared unfit for human consumption. The Dutch authorities emphasise that, in their view there is no danger to public health from this problem. In the first place because no infectious agent, dangerous to humans, has been detected. In addition, the meat inspection system provides sufficient guarantees for public health. If during this investigation a disease is detected which renders the meat unfit for human consumption, the meat will be declared unfit. The meat will also be declared unfit if the veterinary inspector finds that the meat is abnormal, even though the type of disorder has not been diagnosed. The MVWS, through its Inspectorate for Health Protection, Commodities and Veterinary Public Health (IW&V), is also involved. The main task of this Inspectorate is to enforce and control compliance with regulations on food, consumer articles and veterinary matters through the performance of supervision, detection and investigation activities. The AID is the implementing body of the MLNV that controls and investigates issues related to legislation that fall within the responsibility of the Ministry, as well as general criminal law. Some duties that fall under the responsibility of the MVWS, such as the control of animal disease prevention and eradication aspects of the Meat Inspection Act, are also covered by the AID. At this stage, this service, has not been involved since no legal irregularities have been detected. The animal health services (GD), a private body at the service of the primary agricultural sector, performs many tasks for the Product Boards as well as for the Government. The GD mainly concentrates on the surveillance and diagnosis of animal diseases. It has been given the task by the NZO of carrying out an investigation on the farms identified as having a problem - following guidelines set up by the MLNV DQG 09:6, but has also been involved in the complaint actions set up by the LTO (see next paragraph). The GD operates with inspectors and three diagnostic laboratories, which perform routine analysis on the most common non- notifiable livestock diseases. INTRODUCTION The mission to the Netherlands was the fifth of a series of inspections to all Member States to audit the plant health system in the potato sector. A pre-mission questionnaire was sent to the Dutch plant protection authorities in advance of the mission. The answers to this questionnaire provided an overview of the Dutch plant health system in the potato sector and of the general health status of the potato production in the Netherlands.

MISSION DETAILS The mission in the Netherlands took place from 3 to 7 July 2000. The mission team comprised 2 inspectors from the Food and Veterinary Office (FVO), and 2 Member State experts. Representatives from the Dutch plant protection service accompanied the inspection team during the whole mission. An opening meeting was held on 3 July 2000 in Wageningen with the central competent authority. At this meeting, the objectives of, and itinerary for, the mission were confirmed by the inspection team. A closing meeting with the central competent authority was held in Wageningen on 7 July 2000. The following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Competent authority Central 2 Regional 2 LABORATORY VISITS Official laboratories 3 Private laboratories 3 PLANT HEALTH CONTROL SITES Potato breeding/multiplication stations 2 Potato producers 6 Potato packing/despatch stations 2 Potato processing plants 1

OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objectives of the mission were to assess (1) the performance of the various bodies involved in the national plant health system with reference to the potato sector, and (2) the implementation of the relevant EU legislation in this area. 1

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the provisions of Article 19a of Council Directive 77/93/EEC1, last amended by Commission Directive 1999/53/EC2. The legislation (in addition to Council Directive 77/93/EEC) of particular relevance for this mission, was: ­ Council Directive 69/464/EEC3 on the control of potato wart disease, ­ Council Directive 69/465/EEC4 on the control of potato cyst eelworm, ­ Council Directive 93/85/EEC5 on the control of potato ring rot, ­ Council Directive 98/57/EC6 on the control of potato brown rot, ­ Commission Directive 93/50/EEC7 on the registration of producers, warehouses and dispatching centres.
