Previous missions to the Netherlands concerning potatoes During the last five years, the Food and Veterinary Office of the European Commission (FVO) has carried out 4 missions to the Netherlands with relevance to potatoes. All 4 missions focused solely on brown rot (caused by Ralstonia solanacearum) and the subsequent implementation of the Commission Decision on temporary additional measures as regards the Netherlands to prevent the spread of the disease. (Commission Decision 95/506/EC8 as last amended by Commission Decision 98/738/EC9). During these missions, the Netherlands was generally found to be complying with the requirements. 1 OJ No. L 26, 31.1.1977, p. 20 2 OJ No. L 142, 5.6.1999, p. 29 3 OJ No. L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 1 4 OJ No. L 323, 24.12.1969, p. 3 5 OJ No. L 259, 18.10.1993, p. 1 6 OJ No. L 235, 21.8.1998, p. 1 7 OJ No. L 205, 17.8.1993, p. 22 8 OJ No. L 291, 6.12.1995, p. 48 9 OJ No. L 354, 30.12.1998, p. 62 2 5.2. Potato production in the Netherlands In 1998, potato production represented 3.7% of the Netherlands 's gross agricultural output and 7.3% of the gross output in crop production (EUROSTAT). The Netherlands is the second largest producer of potatoes in the EU. Over the last three years, about 180,000ha per year, equivalent to 20-25% of the total cropping area, were grown with potatoes. Yields are generally high; thus, in 1999 a total of 8.2 million tons was produced which means a national average of about 45t/ha. The Netherlands is the EU's largest producer of seed potatoes. Over the last three years, almost 40,000ha of certified seed potatoes were grown per year. 5.3. Potato trade in the Netherlands Seed potatoes The Netherlands has, as an average over the last five years, imported about 19,000t of seed potatoes per year, mainly from Belgium, France and United Kingdom (EUROSTAT). The Netherlands is the largest exporter of seed potatoes in the world. On average over the last five years, 600,000t were exported per year; about 60% to other Member States and 40% to Third Countries (EUROSTAT). Other potatoes The Netherlands is a large importer of potatoes for processing (mainly for chips) and for starch production. Of the 1999 harvest, 1.2 million t were imported, of which 600,000 were for processing, 400,000 for starch production and 200,000 for direct consumption. On average over the last five years, the Netherlands has exported about 900,000 tons per year of ware/industrial potatoes, of which over half went to Germany and Belgium (EUROSTAT). In addition, processed products equivalent to 2-3 million tons of fresh potatoes are exported each year.

MAIN FINDINGS 6.1. Plant health system in the Netherlands 6.1.1. Structure of the plant health system The Plant Health Service (Plantenziektenkundige Dienst = PD) has been designated as the "single and central authority" for plant health as understood in Article 1 (6) of Council Directive 77/93/EEC. The PD is an 3 implementing agency of the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature Management and Fisheries (MANMF), directly under the responsibility of the Minister. The MANMF has the responsibility for plant health legislation and represents the Netherlands at the international level (e.g. the EU Council meetings, FAO, IPPC, Third Countries). The PD deals with technical questions related to plant health and represents the Netherlands in the EU Standing Committee on Plant Health. The PD carries out or supervises all activities related to plant health. Three accredited private institutions cooperate with the PD in potato plant health. The Netherlands General Inspection Service for Agricultural Seed and Seed Potatoes (Nederlandse Algemeine Keuringsdienst = NAK), a private foundation that co-operates closely with the PD, is by far the most important of these institutions. It is in charge of the certification of seed potatoes including the issuing of plant passports. With regards to quarantine organisms, the NAK carries out a substantial share of the screening tests for R. solanacearum and the majority of the laboratory analyses of soil samples for potato cyst nematodes. The two other institutions are private laboratories that are accredited for the soil sampling and analysis for potato cyst nematodes. They do not have any other function in potato plant health. In addition, a third laboratory is in the process of being accredited. 6.1.2. Human and financial resources Human resources In total, the PD headquarters employs around 150 staff (including laboratory personnel). In the 12 district offices, there is about 200 staff. PD management estimates that about 80% of the PD field inspections and laboratory tests are done on potatoes while more than 50% of the total PD resources are dedicated to the potato sector. The NAK has 280 employees, of whom 110 are field staff involved in potato field and seed lot inspection. The NAK estimates that about 45% of its turnover comes from potato inspection and certification. Four years of successful studies at a middle level agricultural school is the minimum educational requirement for plant health inspectors, both at the PD and at the NAK. PD inspectors have access to technical training. NAK inspectors meet once a year for an instruction session. When necessary, the PD organises specific additional training sessions for NAK staff (as e.g. when brown rot occurred). Senior staff at the PD headquarters is entitled to participate in management training courses, which are offered by external institutions. 4 Financial resources The PD is partly funded through the government budget and partly through fees that are charged for inspections and laboratory analyses. The resources are allocated on the basis of an annual work programme, which is prepared by the PD and approved by the MANMF. In the event of an emergency, additional funding can be obtained. The private institutions cooperating with the PD in plant health are funded through cost covering fees paid by the agricultural producers. They do not receive any financial support through the government budget. 6.1.3. Internal or external assessment of the institution's work The MANMF drafts annual strategic work plans in consultation with the PD. The PD then works out detailed task oriented work plans. Due to its agency status, the PD is required to keep the Ministry informed about its activities on a regular basis. Every three months, a review of the work progress and the financial status takes place, in which the director of the PD reports to the management board of MANMF. The NAK has its own quality management system. In addition, the NAK is audited by the PD at least three times a year. The PD produces a report of each audit. 6.1.4. Transposition and enforcement of legislation The transposition of EU Directives related to plant health is done by MANMF in close collaboration with the PD, which provides technical input. Three types of legislation may be used to transpose EU legislation: laws such as the crop protection act, royal decrees, and regulations. Laws must pass parliament and are only used for fundamental changes in the plant health legislation. Royal decrees must be approved by the cabinet, while regulations can be made by the MANMF alone. All directives of relevance for plant quarantine in potatoes have been transposed in the Netherlands. The General Inspection Service (Algemene Inspectie Dienst = AID), which operates under the Minister of Agriculture, is the leading institution with regard to law enforcement in the agricultural sector. Most irregularities in the implementation of plant health legislation are detected by the PD or the NAK, which then pass on the cases to the AID. The AID carries out the formal investigation on the basis of which, a prosecutor decides on corrective measures. The implementation of corrective measures is verified by AID. 5 6.1.5. Contingency plans PD inspectors have a handbook on quarantine organisms. It contains instructions on how to handle brown rot and ring rot outbreaks and details on the sampling procedures within the respective monitoring programmes. 6.2. Seed potatoes in the Netherlands 6.2.1. Potato breeding and seed certification Breeding A gene bank for wild Solanum species and original South American cultivars is held by the Centre for Genetic Resources, within Wageningen University and Research Centre. The collection contains about 1950 accessions of 120 wild species and 750 accessions of 5 primitive species. Cultivated potato varieties are held by breeders. The potato breeding system in the Netherlands is to a large extent based on a system of numerous part or full time "associated breeders" that receive the original clones from a breeding company and then carry out the selection work. The inspection team visited such a company whose varieties constitute 35% of the Dutch seed market. This company handles 140,000 clones per year of which 100,000 are dealt with at its 75 associated breeders. Thus, of the company's variety list, over 95% come from its associated breeders. The company is involved during various stages in the selection process, e.g. for assessing qualities like processing properties or pest resistance that cannot easily be evaluated in the field with traditional methods. Multiplication and production of seed The majority of pre-basic seed still comes from traditional clonal selection done at 600-700 specialised seed farms. However, the use of tissue culture propagation is increasing and is now the basis for about 40% of the pre-basic seed. The material enters at the farm level as minitubers, mainly produced in the Netherlands where there are 7 such producers. The NAK is the largest of these with about half of the total production. The figure below outlines the certification system in the Netherlands. The higher grades of seeds are primarily produced in the northern areas. Certified seed is also grown in the western and central parts of the country. In total there are over 2,600 seed farms in the Netherlands, of which one third grow less than 5ha. 6 The certification is, as mentioned before, done by the NAK. A database has been developed that contains information on all the lots certified or in the process of certification. Data are immediately available for the last four growing seasons. The PD has reading access to this database, which facilitates trace back and forward when quarantine diseases are detected in the seed production. For production and use of farm saved seed, see 6.3.1 below. 6.2.2. Plant health in the breeding and multiplication of seeds 6.2.2.1. Non quarantine pests With regard to the breeding for resistance, Phytophthora infestans (late blight) and Erwinia carotovora (blackleg) have the highest priority of the non-quarantine diseases. In the first stages of the multiplication chain, viruses and other agents are avoided, as mentioned before, mainly by traditional clonal selection of healthy plants and only partly by use of meristem culture techniques. The higher grades of seed potatoes are furthermore grown in coastal areas with low risk of aphid transmission of viruses. 6.2.2.2. Quarantine pests in the breeding material Import permits for material from Third Countries for breeding or scientific purposes are issued on the basis of a written application and if the importer is not well known by the PD, a filled in questionnaire and possible inspection visit to the importer's premises. The material is placed in quarantine either at the PD or, if multiplication is needed to have enough material for the testing, at the NAK. Testing for quarantine potato viruses and viroids is performed on all imports from outside the EU and on all material taken out of the gene bank, if such testing has not been done before. In addition, at least 60 accessions per year from the gene bank are tested as they are being multiplied for maintenance, with the goal of eventually having the whole gene bank tested. In total, around 200 potato accessions are tested each 7 year. During the breeding process, at least at the visited breeding station mentioned in 6.2.1 above, each generation of the material is sampled and tested for both ring rot and brown rot. In general, all potential varieties entering the breeding companies'trials and the official selection are tested for brown rot. After the official selection, all potential varieties are tested for both brown rot and ring rot. 6.2.2.3. Quarantine pests in the multiplication of seed potatoes Brown rot and ring rot Pre-basic material: In the clonal selection system, brown rot testing is done systematically from the third generation of pre-basic seed and in each generation thereafter (there can be up to five generations of pre-basic seed ­ see figure above). Systematic testing for ring rot is done in the third stage only. The minitubers from the tissue culture propagation system enter the regular multiplication scheme as first year clones and are from then subject to the same testing for brown rot and ring rot. In addition, all Dutch initial stock for tissue culture propagation is tested for both brown rot and ring rot. Basic and certified seed: All lots of basic and certified seed are systematically tested for brown rot with at least one sample per 25t. Thus, over the various basic and certified seed grades of the 1999 harvest, a 8 total of 62,452 samples were tested for brown rot. With a total seed potato area of 39,200ha this averages one sample per 0.6ha. As the brown rot testing is obligatory for all seed lots and as such is a part of the certification process, the producers are charged for this testing. For ring rot, surveys are carried out aimed at testing around 10% of the seed lots each year, including all farms that grow grade elite. The selection of seed farms and lots to be tested for ring rot is done centrally by the PD using the NAK database on seed producers. Thus, of the 1999 harvest, 3,806 samples of basic and certified seed were tested in this general survey, giving an average sample density of one sample per 10.3ha. The ring rot tests are paid by the PD. Farm saved seed: Samples are also taken from farm saved seed, produced on the starch potato farms. Thus of the 1999 harvest of about 4,600ha of such farm saved seed, 4,445 samples were tested for brown rot and 952 for ring rot. This is included in the figures in the below tables. Visual inspections (in 1999, around 500) are also carried out. Of all the above samples, 62 (of which 13 came from farm saved seed) tested positive for brown rot. During the field inspections of farm saved seed, 3 cases with visual symptoms were found. Some of the positive samples mentioned came from the same lots, and in total 26 lots were found infected. Some of these lots were again clonally related so that the infections found can be grouped into 14 unrelated "cases" involving 9 varieties: Diamant, Kardal, Bintje, Elkana, Kartel, Desiree, Karakter, Karnico and Seresta. The year before, i.e. 1998 harvest, only two10 samples from certified seed potatoes and three10 from farm saved seed were positive. From the 1997 harvest, 30 samples were found positive. While in the 1998 harvest there was one case of ring rot in seed potatoes, for which the origin could not be determined, all seed samples tested for ring rot of the 1999 harvest were found negative. In addition to the above sampling during the certification process, samples are also taken in exports in response to importing Third Countries' specific requirements. Thus of the 1999 harvest, 1,951 such samples were tested for brown rot and 691 for ring rot. All these samples were negative for both diseases. Recommendations for the active surveillance program · In order to be able to establish the age of cattle to be sampled in the rendering plant an online access to the central bovine database in the sampling area should be provided. · Provisions should be established to ensure that all cattle collected by the rendering plant are identifiable. · It should be considered to collect and transport fallen cattle in vehicles separate from other SRM. · In order to be able to sample the relevant animals in the emergency slaughterhouses it has to be ensured that the age of the animals can be established.

Recommendations on Specified Risk Materials · The competent authorities should issue clear instructions: for the slaughterhouse staff removing Specified Risk Material, aimed at avoiding contamination of carcasses with Specified Risk Material, and as regards workers' protection, Aimed at enabling reconciliation, in particular the keeping of records, and taking due account of the necessary co-operation of the services involved, and monitor these activities. · Procedures should be issued to ensure that the age of cattle to be slaughtered is established before slaughter in order to guarantee that Specified Risk Material is removed from cattle from one year of age. 22

ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT SANCO/3191/2001 Reply of the competent authority to the recommendations in the report The national and regional authorities made very detailed observations about the draft report. The final version of the report was amended to take account of these observations. 5 In response to the recommendations in the report, the national authorities said that they did not intend to amend national legislation in those cases where the inspection team felt that it did not comply with Community legislation. They confirmed, however, that certain steps had been taken or were planned. These included: improving contacts between the Central Government and the Autonomous Communities, including holding two to three meetings each year between the Ministries of Agriculture and Health and the regional authorities to discuss and resolve problems associated with the monitoring of milk production, drawing up a report on the difficulties encountered in mountainous regions, remedying the specific shortcomings identified in the establishments visited during the mission and in all dairy establishments, clarifying the situation with regard to the accreditation of laboratories, trying to resolve the problems which had not yet been resolved with regard to raw milk products in Galicia. The authorities in Cantabria said that certain steps had been taken or were planned in response to the recommendations in the report. These included the following: The guidelines provided by the central authority would be implemented with regard to the criteria relating to the quality of milk. Checks of farms which did not comply with the rules would be stepped up. A warning system had been set up for those cases where inhibitors were found in milk. Official visits would be made to farms where positive results had been obtained. Tests would be carried out more frequently to check for somatic cells and farmers would be given the results. Water from wells on farms would be tested more frequently. Contacts with the other official regional authorities and with the central competent authorities would be improved. A programme of random sampling would be implemented on farms by the operators of dairy establishments under the supervision of the official authorities. The authorities in Cantabria supplied additional guarantees concerning the independence and training of veterinary inspectors, the recruitment of staff, the resources available to the official authorities and monitoring procedures on farms. 6 The authorities in Galicia explained why they believed that some milk products were not subject to the requirements of Community legislation. The authorities in Navarra provided a copy of their official food sampling programme for 2001. They also confirmed that certain steps had been taken or were planned in response to the observations, conclusions and recommendations in the report. 7

INTRODUCTION Estonia is on the provisional list of third countries allowed to export milk and milk-based products to the European Union (Commission Decision 95/340/EC). The mission took place from 28 May to 1 June 2001. The mission team comprised three inspectors from the Food and Veterinary Office (FVO) and one national expert. The mission was undertaken as part of the FVO's planned mission programme, and was the first mission in Estonia specifically on the dairy sector. The inspection team was accompanied during the whole mission by several representatives from the Veterinary and Food Board, the central competent authority (CCA). An opening meeting was held on 28 May 2001 with the CCA. At this meeting, the objectives of, and itinerary for, the mission were confirmed by the inspection team, and additional information required for the satisfactory completion of the mission requested. 2. OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The objective of the mission was to carry out an evaluation of the performance of the official services to guarantee that the health rules for the production and placing on the market of milk and milk-based products intended for export to the EU are at least equivalent to those laid down in Chapter II of Directive 92/46/EEC for Community production. In order to assess the system put in place by the Estonian CA, visits to the different levels of the CA, some of the establishments approved for export to the EU, as well as related official laboratories and dairy farms were performed. In pursuit of this objective, the following sites were visited: COMPETENT AUTHORITY VISITS Comments 1 Competent Central 1 authority Regional 4 milk plant laboratories LABORATORY VISITS 3 Private Public 1 LIVE ANIMAL CONTROL SITES Farms FOOD PROCESSING 4 ESTABLISHMENTS - there are no milk collection centres in Estonia Milk processing premises Collection centre 7 3. LEGAL BASES The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries1. · Council Directive 92/46/EEC of 16 June 1992 laying down the health rules for the production and placing on the market of raw milk, heat-treated milk and milk based products2. 4. BACKGROUND 4.1. Previous related missions to Estonia There were two previous OICVP/FVO missions to Estonia, related to milk and milk products. The first (XXIV/2241/97) was carried out in October 1997. While the animal health situation in relation to milk and milk products was considered satisfactory, the public health inspection of the establishments proposed by the Estonian CCA was unsatisfactory. The second mission (XXIV/1412/98) was carried out from 9 to 12 June 1998 as follow-up to the previous one. During this mission, the performance of the CCA was assessed, and one dairy plant, visited previously in 1997, was inspected, as well as one integrated slaughterhouse, cutting and meat processing plant. The outcome of the visits was satisfactory for the dairy plant but unsatisfactory for the meat plant. The report of this mission is available under its specific reference number on the DG (Health and Consumer Protection) internet site at http://europa.eu.int/comm/food/fs/inspections/index_en.html 4.2. MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Legislation 5.1.1. General The main legal acts in Estonian legislation, relevant for this mission, are the following: 10 · Food Act of 25 February 19993, as amended · Veterinary Act ( Veterinaarkorralduse seadus) of 16 June 19994 · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No. 28 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for the Production of Milk and Milk Products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.30 of 21st October 1999 on Hygiene Requirements for Producing Raw Milk in a Dairy Farm · Veterinary and Food Inspectorate Directive No. 35 of 15th November 2000 on requirements for veterinary certificates and certification · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.44 of 24th December 1999 on veterinary requirements for importation of animals and animal products · Minister of Agriculture Regulation No.12 of 16th of March 5 ("Statutes of the Veterinary and Food Board") An extensive list of Estonian legal acts, corresponding to EC legal acts relevant for this mission is attached after the table of content. The mission team noted that amongst the large number of recently (1995- 2001) adopted Estonian legal acts related to the objective of the mission, two ­ Raw Milk Hygiene Regulation no 30 of 1999, and Milk and Milk Products Hygiene Regulation, no 28 of 1999 ­ refer officially to the relevant EC legislation (Council Directives 92/46/EEC, 89/362/EEC, 89/384/EEC, 94/71/EEC and 95/165/EEC). 5.1.2. Equivalence of Estonian legislation An initial assessment of the Estonian legislation revealed that certain provisions of the Community legislation relevant for the current mission had no equivalent in the Estonian legislation: · no approval required for heat treatment equipment · no formal requirement for official recognition of laboratories carrying out analysis about own-check samples · no official registration of farms supplying milk to EU-premises. 3 RT (= Riigi Teataja, State Gazette) I 1999, 30, 415 4 RT I 1999, 58, 608 5 RTL 2000, 38, 535 11 · no procedure for the withdrawal of farms supplying milk not fulfilling EC requirements In addition, there were no administrative measures in place to ensure that EU exports met these requirements. With regard to quality of raw milk, the current Estonian legislation requires a plate count of 500,000/ml or less, and a somatic cell count of 500,000/ml or less, in raw cow's milk (c.f. chapter 5.4.2). One standard of milk is officially acknowledged. However, in one EC approved plant, the mission team was told by the management that the old system based on the Soviet GOST is still used "internally"- for domestic production. This system comprises three standards of milk: superior, first and unclassified (out ­of-standard). 5.2. CA structure and organisation The Central Competent Authority for matters related to the production, collection and processing of milk in Estonia is the Veterinary and Food Board, Veterinaar- ja Toiduamet (formerly Veterinary And Food Inspection Service, the name changed in 2000). The VFB is working under the Ministry of Agriculture and the Chief Veterinary Officer reports to the Minister of Agriculture. 5.2.1. Management structure The structure of the CCA is described in details in the report XXIV/1412/98 and has not changed since that time. It is a pyramidal structure with direct line of command. 5.2.2. Independence All the officials responsible for the performance of inspections and supervision of establishments enjoy an employment status that guarantees their independence from the establishments for which they are responsible. The staff are paid by the Ministry of Agriculture, but the budget is allocated by the Parliament and cannot be changed by the Ministry. No other occupations for the staff are authorised, unless permitted by the Director (CVO for the CCA and the Director of the Regional Veterinary Centre for the provincial staff). 5.2.3. Resources The budget of the VFB is currently 64 000 000 EEK (ca 11 636 363 ). It is 30 % tax-funded, allocated by the Parliament through the Ministry of Agriculture, together with supervision fees from the food industry, import fees and meat inspection fees. The staff of the VFB is 334 in total, 32 of them in the HQ in Tallinn (20 veterinarians and 12 administrative staff including central bookkeeping). This also includes 118 staff of the Border Inspection Service, 15 of them 12 in the HQ in Tallinn. There are currently vacancies within the VFB, but this is not considered as a problem. The CVO finds the staffing situation satisfactory. 5.2.4. Recruitment & training 5.2.4.1.Recruitment Staff are recruited on the basis of public competition, as required by the Law on Public Service of the 25 January 1995. A yearly accreditation (review) is carried out of all staff members by the Director (and of the Director by a governmental commission). The mission team was told that in one case, accreditation was delayed for six months for one regional VFB director. In addition to officials, there are a number of authorised veterinarians, i.e. private practitioners employed by the VFB on a contract basis. They may be contracted by the CCA for the performance of some official tasks, e.g. TB testing, vaccination or monitoring of hygiene on the farms. The contract is for 1 year, but may be extended for up to 5 years, depending upon the budget situation. There are currently 209 authorised veterinarians in Estonia. All veterinary practitioners in Estonia have to be licensed by the Veterinary and Food Board. To obtain a licence, the following is required: a veterinary diploma, a certificate from the regional VFB and evidence of additional training. A licence is valid for 5 years, and a list of licensed veterinarians is kept by the CCA. Currently, there are 852 licensed veterinarians in Estonia. Steps have been taken to remind the control services (instructions dated 20 November 2001) of the obligations on the industry as regards denaturing SRM. In addition, the risks of superficial contamination of carcasses by spinal 31 cords on their removal have also been identified by the health authorities. This gave rise to an amendment to the Order of 17 March 1992 concerning the requirements to be met by slaughterhouses for the production and placing on the market of fresh meat and laying down the conditions for the health inspection of such establishments (amendment introduced by the Order of 19 July 2001); it requires removal of the spinal cord of bovines aged 12 months and over prior to cutting the carcass into halves by splitting the vertebral column. This requirement, which entered into force on 1 January 2002 in all bovine slaughterhouses, now precludes, on the one hand, the risk of nervous tissue spreading onto the carcass after splitting and, on the other, contamination of the muscle masses next to the vertebral column when the cord is removed manually both by the operators and by the equipment used. 2. As far as the rules are concerned, the requirement to incinerate the vertebral columns of bovines aged 12 months and over was introduced by the Order of 2 October 2001. The formal classification as SRM was officialised by the Order of 4 January 2002. (These two Orders are amendments to the Order of 17 March 1992.) 3. The French authorities ensure that all "low-risk" meal and fats are incinerated. Although, pending establishment of specific collection in the so-called "high- risk" channel of vertebral columns of bovines aged 12 months and over, notably collection from butchers, these products were treated with "low-risk" waste, the Community requirement, that is the incineration of vertebral columns, will be complied with. The French authorities authorise only two types of disposal for the meal produced, direct incineration or storage pending incineration. No processing, including into so-called technical products, is permitted. Furthermore bearing in mind the special requirement in France for a specific dedicated procedure for the production of processed animal protein intended for petfood (as meal from ruminants is prohibited to ensure that there is no cross- contamination resulting from the existence of several channels) and the ban on the use of meal from ruminants in fertiliser production, the only type of disposal for all meal (high and low risk) is incineration. 4. Retaining two channels, high and low risk, could be unwarranted in so far as all products are disposed of by incineration. However, given the limited incineration capacity, the French authorities wanted to retain this separation to ensure priority for just-in-time incineration of TSE risk products and to store only the others. For the special case of the vertebral column, inclusion in the high-risk sector without preparation, notably as regards setting in place new logistics and the selective sorting of bones in the cutting plant, might have resulted in a requirement to store meal also containing dead animals and all SRM. It therefore appeared preferable to store meal containing only bovine vertebral columns, rather than meal containing all SRM, naturally requiring in all cases ultimate incineration 32

Official controls In general, the official controls should be more targeted in the areas of inspection visits and the follow up actions strengthened in the premises. This should also include random official sampling, at establishments' level, to verify and confirm the reliability of the analyses performed by the companies in the framework of their "own-checks" plans.

Monitoring programme on bivalve molluscs The RVV should organise a system of supervision of the PV as regards the activities linked to the bivalve molluscs sector. The RVV should also establish a formal protocol regarding the procedures of laboratories performing analyses linked to monitoring programmes on bivalve molluscs, in particular for bacteriological and biotoxins determination. Written evidence of these interrelations should be recorded. It is recommended that the number of sampling points for the routine monitoring on biotoxins/phytoplankton and microbiological aspects in the re-watering plots should be increased. The laboratory methods for microbiological and biotoxins analyses should be those laid down in the relevant EU legislation and recommended by the Community Reference Laboratories (CRLs). The samples for phytoplankton analyses should be taken using an integrated method to ensure that the total water column is sampled. A tube sample or a vertical net haul should be used, especially in areas where the water stratifies.

Sites visited The deficiencies observed by the inspection team in the plants visited should be rectified; in particular the traceability of products and the correct use of the official health mark should be strictly supervised during official inspections. Laboratories All laboratories performing official analyses should be accredited. The CA should also approve establishments' internal laboratories. The CA should recognise laboratories performing analyses for checking the efficiency of purification of bivalve molluscs. Co-ordination should be established between the NRLs and all the regional laboratories performing official analyses sited on the CCAA where the production areas of bivalve molluscs are declared. Spain should inform the Commission services of the actual date of designation of the NRL for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs. Official control 8.1.3.1.Fishery products The Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures in cases where the relevant requirements of approval of establishments and factory vessels cease to be met. The guides produced by the central and regional services visited for the approval and assessment of HACCP systems should be put into force. Pending adoption of Community provisions, those issued by the central authorities for controls over Listeria monocytogenes in smoked fishery products should at least be respected. The Real Decreto 202/2000, for the supervision of staff handling foodstuffs, should be implemented. In order to avoid any risk of possible fraudulent imports of fishery products from TCs, the system of bilateral agreements in place should take into consideration the information produced by the TC authorities and by FVO missions. 8.1.3.2.Bivalve molluscs The relevant Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures to guarantee that bivalve molluscs are put on the market only if they are harvested in officially declared production areas where the respective 25 classification and monitoring of phytoplankton, microbiological and marine biotoxins contamination are put in place. The registration documents should be amended, in accordance with the relevant requirements, in all the purification/dispatch centres visited. All the relevant marine biotoxins (PSP, DSP and ASP) should be checked in all bivalve molluscs, gastropods, echinoderms and tunicates harvested. The Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures in cases where the relevant requirements of approval purification/dispatch centres cease to be met.

As far as the outbreak of Ralstonia solanacearum is concerned Portugal states that "Given the characteristics of the farms and production systems in the areas where outbreaks of infection with the bacteria were detected, it was not always possible, despite the great efforts made, to precisely identify the origin of the contamination and, therefore, to successfully carry out all the surveys that were needed. Whenever infected potato fields were found, the quarantine measures required under the Directive were taken. In the case of fields that were probably contaminated, it was decided to subject them to more intensive official checks, stepping up inspection of the crops growing there. As regards contaminated irrigation water, the fact that laboratory tests on samples collected from the same watercourse at different dates often produced both positive and negative results made it difficult to have a clear overview of the situation and to take the radical step of banning irrigation. However, the Authorities kept the situation under control, issuing circulars drawing attention to the risk to plants and recommending that the water not be used to irrigate solanacea crops".
Portugal will devise a contingency plan by the end of this year to deal with any future outbreak of Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus. A copy of the plan will then be sent to the Commission.

Taking account of existing laboratory capacity, Portugal will make an attempt this year to adapt the control plan by increasing the number of tests carried out on Portuguese ware potatoes in order to detect Ralstonia solanacearum.
An attempt will be made to increase the official supervision of the PCN tests processed by the accredited body. 25

Generalities related to CA FP/LBM control system performance As recommended in the previous mission report all relevant legislation should be fully and properly implemented and enforced by the DCMNR. In order to achieve this goal, the setting up of the announced Specialised Food Safety Unit and the compatibility of the food safety and fisheries control duties dedicated to SFOs should be considered as a priority. Additionally, the programmed increase of the number of qualified staff should continue. The formalisation/documentation of corrective actions and procedures ­ namely those already drafted and distributed to SFOs ­, and in particular in relation to report issuing, should be improved. The deficiencies noted in laboratories carrying out analyses for official and private purposes, including those deficiencies identified by the audits already performed by the FSAI, should be corrected. The DCMNR should check all registered fishing vessels and in particular a solution should be found for the inspection of the factory vessel. The Irish authorities should ensure that the conditions applied to imports of fishery products from the USA (included in part II of the list of Annex to Decision 97/296/EEC) are at least equivalent to those governing the production and placing on the market of Community products, in accordance with Article 11.7 of Directive 91/493/EEC. Drinking water should be used within the meaning of Directive 98/83/EC. Its chlorination should be carefully followed by establishments' staff and assessed by SFOs in order to prevent any possible risk for public health. All deficiencies/shortcomings observed in the establishments visited during the mission should be corrected and the CA should ensure appropriate follow up. This also applies to other establishments where similar situations could be found. 21

Live Bivalve Molluscs The MI should put in place their newly drafted working programme in order to comply with the requirements of Directive 91/492/EEC and of Commission Decision 1999/313/EC. The implementation of these requirements should include the correction of the deficiencies identified in 2.2.1 Laboratories of this report. The use of alternative methods for the detection of Saxitoxin (PSP) - different from the biological testing method - should only be considered after its recognition, in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 12 of Directive 91/492/EEC. The use of alternative chemical methods for the detection of lipophilic toxins - different from the biological testing method - should be considered only after availability of standards for new analogues of public health significance and validation of its performance characteristics following an internationally agreed protocol, in accordance with the requirements of Commission Decision 2002/225/EC. The monitoring for ASP in wild scallops, in particular the transfer of responsibilities from the DCMNR to the private sector should be reviewed according to the requirements of Commission 2002/226/EC. The Irish authorities should undertake the necessary actions in dispatch/purification centres which are not in compliance with the relevant Community requirements. In particular, inspections of dispatch/purification centres, at regular intervals, should be put in place by the Irish authorities, in particular to check the performance of end product testing in accordance with Chapters V of Council Directive 91/492/EEC, and to control establishment own-check HACCP plans developed in accordance with Council Directive 93/43/EEC.

Fishery Products The SFOs should inspect each batch of fishery products at the time of landing or before first sale. Initiatives will be developed to provide better training of staff involved in controls in all of the various areas of activity. Low staffing levels are giving cause for serious concern not only within DGV but also in the regional services. This problem is affecting the entire public administration and DGV will continue to discuss this with its supervising authorities, making it clear that it is hampering our ability to meet our obligations. Although the CCA is fully aware of staff shortages in some areas, a thorough review will be carried out with a view to submitting proposals to make good these shortcomings.

The organisational differences between DGV and other administrative bodies -- specifically DGFCQA ­ in respect of certain common or additional tasks remain to be clarified. 14 DGV stated that correct coordination between the different bodies will be covered by a detailed programme that will include all the appropriate procedures. DGAIEC is currently in contact with DGV, through exchange of correspondence and meetings between experts from the two directorates-general, with a view to examining the implementation of procedures to determine the best way of coordinating activities across all of the departments working in the various areas of responsibility of DGV and DGAIEC. Work is progressing jointly with DGV to develop the mechanisms needed to incorporate, maintain and continuously update the information relating to the CN codes appearing on the positive list annexed to Decision 2002/349/EC and those listed in DGAIEC's Working Tariff (Pauta de Serviço); Code 3101 will be added as soon as possible. The Directorate for Veterinary Control Services has already been in contact with the Directorate for Veterinary Public Health Services -- the department responsible for the residues testing programme -- and a plan covering checks on imported products is already in preparation.

A decision at higher level on the shortcomings affecting checks on customs warehouses and the supervision of kitchen waste is still pending, since the competencies of each of the bodies have still not been clearly defined. Prohibit movement, except under official control, of potato lots with a "suspected occurrence" until the suspicion has been verified/refuted as required in Article 4 (2) (a) of both directives. b. Prescribe measures on all fields of a contaminated place of production as required by Article 5 of the two directives (and specified in detail in Annexes III and IV of the ring rot directive and Annex V and VI of the R. solanacearum directive). c. Carry out thorough investigation along clonal links for each case as required in Article 6 of the ring rot directive and Article 5 of the R. solanacearum directive and take the necessary consequences in the form of designating contamination and probable contamination. Where a clonal link is the most likely cause of the contamination (i.e. separate outbreaks have been found without any other identifiable cause than their common source of seed), at least all sister lots should be designated as "probably contaminated" ­ or, of course, if test results are positive, "contaminated". The farms where this designation has been done - regardless of test results ­ should be included in the "demarcated zone" with the corresponding requirements for surveys, renewal of seed etc.. d. Application of ABP requirements along the chain The ABP requirements are largely applied as described by the CCA. However, some shortcomings were noted: Observations: 9 A frequent finding was the lack of compliance with provisions on labelling and commercial documentation that accompanies category 3 ABP and products therefrom. This applied to many consignments coming from other Member States and frequently for consignments sent from Dutch establishments. Sometimes, no indication was included as regards category of the materials, particularly when the material was an ABP produced from raw material fit for human consumption. Approval numbers for sender and customer were also frequently lacking. Understanding of the need for categorise the material as ABP once its intended use had been decided was not totally clear to all operators in the ABP chain and all official inspectors met. 12 9 In one fat processing plant still approved under previous legislation collecting only category 3 material, deficiencies were noted as regards categorisation of incoming materials with no indication of their category or species of origin. Commercial documents had been stamped with these details at arrival by this plant of destination. Category 3 rendered fats were sent normally to feed establishments and petfood plants. However, two of the customers acting as intermediaries for ABP were plants approved under foodstuffs legislation that had not been approved as intermediaries in the ABP chain (15). 9 In one intermediate plant for category 3 material RVV staff advised the mission team that only 50% of the ANIMO messages sent to Germany accompanying consignments of MBM were being acknowledged at arrival. 9 In a plant approved for processing manure the mission team noted that the operator had recently discontinued the notification to the CA for preparation of ANIMO messages that must accompany consignments of processed manure to other Member States. Allegedly, the reason was the high administrative burden that this placed on their daily operation. In addition, unprocessed dried manure was sent also to other Member States, mainly Germany, always accompanied by a health certificate as agreed beforehand with the CCA of the country of destination. 9 An establishment visited and approved as a technical plant for wool was acting as an intermediary and the mission team noted that raw material was coming from several cattle dealers and farmers. In the first case, no records existed that would have allowed traceability of the farm or region where wool was originally produced. Documents seen for wool coming from individual farms indicated the region of origin. Commercial documentation accompanying the wool to washers in Belgium or France did not include information on ABP as required in Annex II to the ABP Regulation (16). 9 In the food processing establishments visited (meat, milk, retail and wholesale) it was noted that generally there were established systems for handling of ABP. In the meat industry the system was well established in respect of the handling of category 1 and 2 materials. These ABP were mixed together and sent to a category 1 processing plant, as foreseen. Some deficiencies were noted in connection to their handling: (15) In their response to the draft report the Dutch authorities noted that the two customers in question were dealers who collected the material and delivered it to its ultimate destination. These dealers also had their own approved food plant, but the material was not delivered to that address. The ABP Regulation does not stipulate that these dealers must be approved. Approval as an intermediary is not necessary, since the material was not delivered to the food plant and since the approval requirements (building and hygiene requirements) are not applicable to a dealer. The VD recognises this problem and is considering ways of addressing it. The error here was that the wrong destination was given on the commercial documentation. The firms do this deliberately for commercial reasons, as they do not want the recipient/customer to know where the material was purchased from. Training of BIP staff was performed on 18.-22.10.2004. and 22.-26.11.2004., including training on listed BIP facilities and TRACES. Compulsory training on TRACES will take place on 22 December 2004. In addition, the training focused more on improvement of skills of inspectors to make them sufficiently familiar with the documentation system. A new "check list", needed for supervision of veterinary inspection posts and for monitoring was approved on 10.12.2004. From January 1, 2005 it is planned to set up a veterinary sector at the Quality Ensuring Division on the SBI central level. In Ventspils, changes in the number of staff will depend on the flow of consignments.

The Central Customs Office in its letter No 16.1.4./33292 dated December 9, 2004 informed the Sanitary Border Inspection regarding access to the customs database that currently, legal formalities are being coordinated between the Legal Department and Informatics Department of the State Revenues Service, at present the programs are being tested. It is not possible to fix the final date at this stage.

The formal approval document was issued by CCA on 11 October 2004 with the relevant legal basis. Updated cooperation agreement with customs warehouse owner signed on 11 November 2004. All gaps regarding Art. 12 of Directive 97/78/EC are corrected on 11 November 2004. Updated information concerning "special economic free zones" is published on the internet on 06.12.2004 on customs website in Latvian. The information will be soon translated into English.

text: In free zones in Riga Port and Ventspils, the gates will be moved in order to include the BIP facilities. 12 The gates have been physically moved and they will start functioning as soon as the BIP is included in the list. Activities of the BIP and activities of the warehouse are fully separated. Minor deficiencies regarding hygiene are rectified: a) Ventspils: no more hand -operable tabs in inspection rooms, one drain is completely sealed. b) Daugavpils: no more hand ­operable tabs in hygienic sluice and inspection rooms, dispensers for hand disinfection are obtained, no more wooden cleaning equipment. c) Rezekne: no more hand ­operable tabs in inspection rooms, open spaces in inspection room, different levels in unloading area are corrected. d) Riga port: no more hand ­operable tabs in inspection rooms, routing of staff in changing room is corrected. Baltmarine Terminal: Activities of the BIP and of the warehouse are fully separate: storage room no 3 for EU conforming goods, storage room no 4 for EU non- conforming goods and ramps no 1, 2 are foreseen for BIP use; storage room no 2 for EU non-conforming goods and ramps no 3, 4 are foreseen for warehouse use. Regarding supervision of customs warehouses and non-compliances of records kept by ship suppliers in Ventspils, Daugavpils, Rezekne have been corrected. For Ventspils kitchen waste is not allowed to be loaded, and captain signs a declaration that waste is not loaded, similarly as it is in Riga.
Pre-notification according to Article 7(1) of Directive 97/78/EC is requested for all arriving consignments.
Posters in Riga airport and information for railway passengers reflect correctly provisions of Regulation (EC) No.745/2004 now.

Information regarding non-commercial movements of pets is provided as foreseen in Regulation (EC) No.998/2003. All changes are duly notified to the customs regularly by means of e-mail and letters. 12. See comments under point 7.

To consider whether further actions are required in relation to the translation error in the Spanish version of Council Directive 91/496/EEC.

ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7352/2004 In response to the recommendations in the draft report, the CAs indicated the followi s under point 8: With regard to the findings or deficiencies detected during the mission carried out last August, CCA have begun to rectify some of the more general problems. 1. The Royal Decree 1976/2004 of 1 October, incorporating Directive 2002/99/EC into national law was published on 15 October 2004. 3. A letter was sent to State Ports, highlighting the need to provide information to inspection posts' veterinary services concerning the arrival of goods in Spanish ports and a meeting has been scheduled during the week from 22 to 26 November between State Ports and the Subdirectorates-General for Animal Health (Ministry of Agriculture), Border Health Controls (Ministry of Health) and Coordination of Local Administration (Ministry of Public Administrations). At that meeting, plans to link BIPs to the PORTEL project, a computer application to manage cargo manifests, will be discussed in more detail. 4. A letter has been sent to DG SANCO on 02.11.2004 requesting to include a new ANIMO unit in the Commission Decision 2002/459/EC for the future BIP in the Castellón port and from 1 January 2005 separating existing codes for BIPs in Valencia port and airport, which have the same code.

MSC and MAPA provided information concerning staff of Spanish BIPs. 7. For legislation, since 29.10. 2004 SA website mapya.es/es/ganaderia/pags/ CEXGAN/cesgan/ has been in operation. All the legislation relating to conditions for importing live animals and products of animal origin not intended for human consumption can be consulted on the MAPA page, as well as in the BIP records. 8. With regard to the BIP of Castellón a. The BIP records contain copies of training course attendance certificates for inspectors assigned to the future BIP in the Port of Castellón. The course in the field of Border Health Controls will be held on 2, 3 and 4 November for veterinary inspectors. Also a veterinary inspector from the BIP in Castellón will attend the course. b. The administrative offices of the SA and SE veterinary services have sufficient archive capacity for the necessary documentation, purchased by the Castellón Port Authority. c. The BIP inspection room has been fitted with the equipment necessary to carry out the appropriate physical inspections for the category of authorisation of this BIP. d. The necessary measures have been taken to rectify minor deficiencies, ensuring that there are disinfectant dispensers in the inspection room, pedal-operated hand wash basin in unloading area and protective meshes against insects at all windows. The inspectors have been equipped with working clothes and a cleaning, disinfection and pest control programme for BIP facilities to be supervised by the inspectors has been presented. e. The documentation required in Decision 2001/812/EC has been provided, i.e.: ­ legislation relating to veterinary inspections and specifically to conditions for importing products of animal origin 13 ­ instructions from the departments ­ lists of authorised establishments ­ lists of accredited laboratories ­ lists of plants dealt with in by-product legislation ­ list of laboratories to which samples may be sent. f. The BIP relies on the appropriate documentation and access to CEXGAN and SANEXTE, computer applications in the field of records. g. CCA has made it possible for the veterinary services to have access to the PORTEL application, offering them computerised access to cargo manifests.

ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7353/2004 In response to the recommendations in the draft report under point 8, the CA indicated the following measures taken to rectify deficiencies: 1. VARS will suggest amendment of the Veterinary Practice Act in order to rectify established deficiencies in the legal order. A final date of adoption of the Amendment Act will depend on the parliamentary adoption procedure itself. VARS will suggest adoption of the Act following the shortened procedure.
Improved by the preparation of written records, control records, data filing, and the system of communication between the BIPs and the Main Office of VARS (via VARS web portal).

VARS shall notify the Slovenian Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Energy (MESP), which is competent for the implementation of Council Regulation (EC) No. 338/97, of the necessary amendment and/or harmonisation of the list of BIPs of entry with the list of BIPs detailed in Commission Decision 2001/881/EC. The list of CITES-consignments, which the border veterinary checks have been prescribed for and which may be imported via the BIPs only that are listed in Commission Decision 2001/881/EC, will need to be amended as well. The public will be notified of any current inconsistencies via the VARS web portal, and of the CITES-consignments (live animals and products), which may enter the territory of the EU via the BIPs only that are listed in Commission Decision 2001/881/EC.

Within the deadline stipulated above and in cooperation with the customs authorities we will publish a list of entry points for pets on the VARS web portal. The list will be communicated to the European Commission and the other Member States.

Training of BIP staff shall be carried out on the basis of a training programme already prepared by the Main Office of VARS in the form of workshops and study tours for border veterinary inspectors to be carried out during 2005. The VARS shall prepare and conduct training programmes for the customs and forwarding agency staff at local level (5 BIPs). The main purpose of trainings will be to harmonise procedures carried out by all the services involved in veterinary controls, and to introduce any new procedures in the operations of these services. An assessment of adequacy of such training will be incorporated in each training session.

Main Office of VARS is in close contact with the General Customs Administration of the Republic of Slovenia, as regards the implementation of necessary checks on consignments of animal origin, animals and personal luggage entering the EU from third countries. In cooperation with VARS, customs authorities have published a brochure containing instructions for passengers entering the EU. See also points 5 and 13.

Main Office of VARS will improve the system for the supervision and monitoring of the operation of the BIPs, in particular with regard to the application of the procedures laid down in Directives 91/496/EEC and 97/78/EC and the associated Regulations and Decisions.

Main Office of VARS will adapt the monitoring plan for import consignments of tests for the presence of residues, pathogens and contaminants for each individual BIP within the deadline referred to above. 12

Approval of co-incinerators is within the competence of the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning (MESP), in accordance with the regulations on environmental protection and according to Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002.The MBM co-incinerator was approved for operation and entered on the list of temporarily approved establishments according to Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002. Establishment was re- approved in December 2004 in accordance with the prescribed approval procedure.

With regard to the infrastructure in Obrezje we have notified the Joint Services of the Government of the Republic of Slovenia, responsible for the construction and equipment of BIPs, of the deficiencies noted at the BIP of Obrezje, and of the deadline for their rectification.
The deficiencies noted for equipment, hygiene, documentation, registration and records at the BIP of Obrezje will be rectified by the stipulated deadline.
The deficiencies noted at the BIP of Gruskovje will be rectified before the deadline for approval of this BIP by the VARS inspection commission.

For the BIP staff to have an overview of all the veterinary consignments arriving at the BIP, we will prepare regular meetings with the customs services and forwarding agencies. The latter will be trained in consignment prenotification procedures. See also points 5 and 6.

Documentary checks on consignments of non-animal origin, in particular of animal feed and veterinary medicinal products, are carried out by the official veterinarians at imports, in accordance with the national legislation. Checks on consignments are not carried out in the facilities of veterinary BIPs.

Procedures of veterinary checks, including laboratory tests in accordance with EU legislation, will be improved by the additional training of border veterinary inspectors and on the basis of the new BIP Manual.

Checks on personal luggage are within the responsibility of the customs services and are carried out in accordance with the requirements of the Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. Border official veterinarians supervise the implementation of such checks.
Jointly with customs authorities, we will improve the BIP system of supervising transiting consignments when leaving the EU.
Implementation is conditional on the amendment of the Veterinary Practice Act, and the Amendment Act will include inspection fees as well. See also point 1. ________________________________
Take urgent measures to ensure that disinfection principles and procedures (as described in Annex II of Council Directive 2002/60/EC) are known, correctly applied and documented;

Ensure close cooperation among the various administrative and professional bodies (at national, regional and local level) which may play a role in prompt and efficient implementation of the control measures related to the control of ASF, and ensure that those responsible all share the same view about the priority which has to be given to this aim;

Ensure that local human resources and equipment are adequate for a complete and strict implementation, supervision and control of the measures to be taken in case of suspicion or confirmation of outbreaks of ASF; apply and control corrective actions in case of identification of deficiencies; 33 In their comments to the draft report the CA of Sardinia stated that the problem of identifying meat that is eligible for movements outside the territory of Sardinia is resolved by internal procedures, validated by the competent veterinary service and adopted by the various slaughterhouse facilities. These provide for various measures : separate slaughter of pigs eligible for movements outside Sardinia (in some cases also separate slaughtering days), storage of meat in separate store rooms, locking these rooms under the supervision of the OV, shipment of eligible meat only after the health certificate to be drawn up on loading has been issued. 26

Ensure a rapid and complete transmission of information to all the concerned bodies, including the European Commission and other countries, in line with the provisions of Council Directive 82/894/EEC and article 3 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC;

Set up and implement an action plan to regularise the situation regarding holding registration and movement control at least in conformity with Council Directive 92/102/EEC; update the register database in accordance with provisions of Commission Decision 2000/678/EC so that it can be used for the determination of restriction zones and its control;

Implement a comprehensive eradication plan for the feral pig population in accordance with article 16 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC, integrating the possible links with free-ranging pigs, the results of the serosurveillance campaigns in wild boars, and investigation about possible vectors;

Ensure that carcasses and fresh meat obtained from pigs which do not fulfil the requirements of Commission Decision 2003/514/EC are not given the health mark provided for in Chapter XI of Annex I of the Directive 64/433/EEC, as stated in Council Directive 72/461/EEC;
Apply control measures over catering waste, as required by article 24 of Council Directive 2001/89/EC;
Revise the system of compensation for owners of pigs slaughtered in accordance with Council Directive 2002/60/EC so as to ensure a swift but adequate compensation;

Consider the development of a comprehensive and detailed action plan for eradication of ASF in Sardinia, addressing all the identified critical points and evaluating the resources needed. To fully implement Council Directive 96/43/EC without delay;
To take action to ensure that the annual NRCP and the results of the previous year's NRCP are submitted to the Commission Services within the deadlines specified in Council decision 96/23/EC;
To take data on VMP usage into account when planning the NRCP;
To ensure a more even spread of sample collection for each analyte throughout the year;
To take action to reduce the times between sample collection and availability of confirmed results in order to facilitate effective follow-up of non- complaint results;
To ensure that the targeted approach is used for collection of samples under the NRCP and that all sampling is unforeseen and unexpected;
To ensure that staff carrying out sampling are instructed to take suspect samples when appropriate; 21
To ensure that all samples collected under the NRCP are stored, sealed and transported in such a way as to ensure sample security at all stages between collection and receipt at the laboratory;
To improve the system of central monitoring and control over the sampling activities carried out by the Prefectural Veterinary Directorates;
To provide sufficient staff and appropriate equipment to ensure that all analytes included in the NRCP are analysed as planned;
To ensure that the consumables necessary for the laboratories to carry out analyses under the NRCP can be obtained as required;
To ensure that all laboratories carrying out analyses for the NRCP become accredited to ISO 17025 within the shortest possible timeframe;
To validate all methods of analyses for A Group substances to the standards required in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC within the shortest possible timeframe;

To develop an action plan to ensure that all analyses for B Group substances will be validated to the standards required in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC within the deadlines specified in that Decision;

To ensure that all laboratories carrying out analyses under the NRCP implement quality assurance measures necessary to ensure the reliability of analytical results, as foreseen in Commission Decision 2002/657/EC;
To provide sufficient resources to ensure that the NRLs can fulfil all requirements as laid out in Article 14 of Council Directive 96/23/EC;
To ensure that sufficient finance is available to allow laboratory staff to receive adequate training and, in particular, to ensure that NRL staff can always participate in relevant CRL workshops;
To ensure that only VMPs with active substances included in either Annexes I, II or III of Council Regulation (EEC) No 2377/90 are authorised for use in food producing animals;
To ensure that an updated list of all authorised VMPs is available to the relevant competent authorities and all persons involved in distribution, prescription or dispensing of VMPs;

To ensure that manufacturing of medicated feedingstuffs takes place in accordance with the requirements of Council Directive 90/167/EC. 9. Modify the presentation of the plan to Commission services, clearly indicating screening and confirmatory methodologies.
Expand the scope of testing in the plan taking account of actual laboratory capability in the SGL and any other pertinent factors in order to have as comprehensive a programme as possible.

The CA has stated that the Directorate-General for International Affairs has decided to incorporate the management of the residue control plans in 2006 into its computer system (SIGAL). Using the SIGAL database, a system to monitor the rate of plan implementation during the year will be established together with schedules to make it easier to follow the sampling carried out by the DDSVs and the observance of their submission and analysis deadlines. Recommendation 2 Regarding the scope of testing and the inclusion of all necessary substance groups, the CA points out that it relies on the National Reference Laboratory and the National Agency for Veterinary Medicinal Products to advise on issues such as method availability, analysis feasibility and the relevance of this research in France, in view of the use made of veterinary medicinal products for these species. In the case of nitroimidazoles these may be tested for in sheep using the LC-MS-MS method, which is already widespread as a confirmatory method and that TLC could be discontinued as a screening method to increase the performance of the control plan. For coccidiostats (B2b), work is under way to develop an LC-MS-MS method to monitor ionophores. This method will be tested in 2006 on study protocols for chicken livers and eggs. The aim of the method development plan is to establish a multi-family method or several methods covering the majority of molecules for 2008. For coccidiostats used in lambs and kids, a method derived from the one which is currently under development for poultry will be finalised in 2007. For coccidiostats, the LERMVD assumed responsibility for additives just a few years ago. The methodological developments (work by the CRL and other NRLs) in this field of activity, which covers various substance families of different chemical makeup, are being followed very closely by the NRL, as are the MRL proposals made by EFSA. Over the next two years, the NRL will able to improve monitoring in this field under its work plan. Considering the substances authorised within the country but which are currently not tested for (e.g. lasalocid and nicarbazin (poultry and eggs), benzimidazoles (pigs), sulphonamides (horses); quinolones (pigs and bovine) and phenylbutazone (milk and pigs), the CA has stated that the same factors (as described above) need to be considered and they are studying the possibility of including these substances in the 2006 NRCP. Specifically the existing methods for benzimidazoles, sulphonamides and quinolones will also be used for the specified species in 2006. The method under development for ionophore coccidiostats will be used as part of the 2006 NRCP. The use of phenylbutazone in muscle is currently being validated and will be widespread by 2006. Its extension to milk will be tested under a study protocol and introduced in 2006. 18 A detection method for avermectins is being developed and will be used for milk under a study protocol in 2006. Regarding the analysis of nitroimidazoles, the NRL proposes reviewing its position (for example, the discontinuation of TLC screening) once an MRPL has been published for nitroimidazoles (so far, an MRPL of 3µg/kg has been proposed by the CRL in Berlin). Metronidazole will be added to the list of molecules in the nitroimidazole family at the time of the request to reopen the 2005 session of the Residue Application. An LC-MS-MS method for the detection and confirmation of nitroimidazoles was used within the framework of the NRL work plan and validated in accordance with Regulation 2002/657. This method will be introduced and possibly replace the current screening method upon publication of the MRPL for these molecules. Tests for sulphonamides and tylosin in honey are currently being developed. For nitrofurans in honey, the NRL is waiting for the results of work ongoing in the UK before adapting the method. For nitrofurans in milk, the method can be adapted for the purposes of monitoring total residues. An addition to the method will be proposed. A new method for analysis of beta-agonists has been developed using Molecular Imprinting Polymer purification with LC-MS-MS in electrospray positive mode. This will allow CRL-recommended limits to be met whilst maintaining broad spectrum screening of numerous beta-agonists. Ensure that comprehensive guidance is provided on checking the requirements of Directive 91/630/EEC in particular those introduced by amendments in 2001.

Ensure that comprehensive guidance is provided on checking the requirements of Directive 99/74/EC, as previously recommended in report 7230/2004, in particular on determining the maximum capacity for each building and the slope of cages.

Ensure that when a deficiency in relation to EU requirements is detected: a. The details of the infringement are adequately recorded including, where Directive 99/74/EC is applicable, the precise location of the flock. b. As previously recommended in report 3344/2001, that effective follow-up action is undertaken in as short a time frame as possible. In particular, urgent action should be taken to address problems with overstocking of laying hens. c. All infringements in relation to EU minimum standards are reliably reported (Article 6 of Directive 98/58/EC and Decision 2000/50/EC).

Ensure that travelling times for poultry meet the maximum journey time laid down in Chapter II of the Annex to Directive 91/628/EEC. In particular, in the case of spent hens, further consideration should be given regarding their fitness for the intended journey (Article 3 (1)(b) Directive 91/628/EEC). ________________________________________ 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7548/2005 In their comments on a draft version of this report the central competent authority indicated: 10 (1) In relation to recommendation 1, that in reply to three motions by political groups, the legal service of the Department is preparing a draft bill concerning animal protection, which it hopes to be present to the Parliament by the end of 2005. (2) In reply to recommendation 2, a document concerning training has been prepared and will be discussed at the co-ordination meeting with the Autonomous Communities on 21 June 2005. In Aragon a draft bill concerning standardisation of training courses has been prepared. (3) In relation to recommendation 3, that the various technical aspects of animal welfare legislation will be dealt with at the meeting of 21 June 2005. The creation of specific working groups for the preparation of guidelines to harmonise animal welfare inspection procedures, for each of the farming species, will be proposed. (4) In reply to recommendation 4, that a working group on the checklist for farm inspections was held during the training course "Minimum requirements for the protection of domestic poultry" (9-11 May 2005). Again this will be discussed at the meeting of 21 June 2005. (5) In relation to recommendations 5 and 6, in order to find solutions to such issues, a distinction will be made between the FVO recommendations referring to specific deficiencies and those deficiencies related to working methods. Again these are for discussion on 21 June 2005 and the CCA believe that the achievement of a national legislation will improve the current situation. 11

The CA should implement the Central Coordinated Project that is aimed to verify and confirm the reliability of the procedures and results from the sampling (LBM and sea water) performed by the fishermen. Information on the progress and results of this project should be forwarded to Commission services.

The CA should ensure that the registration documents accompanying bivalve mollusc batches after harvesting are regularly, uniformly and satisfactorily completed by the fishermen according to the requirements of chapter II, 6 of the Annex to Council Directive 91/492/EEC.

The CA should ensure that reports, and any relevant document transmitted from the laboratories involved in the official control, include the accreditation status of the laboratory (DANAK seal and laboratory accreditation number) and the reference to the analyses correspondent SOP. 01/07/05 - 29145 12
