Generalities related to CA FP/LBM control system performance The following documentation should be forwarded to the Commission services as soon as they are available and, if not finalised at the time of providing the comments to the draft report, detailed information should be provided regarding the situation at that time: - the final version of the protocol between VMM and the FASFC, regarding the provisions for the transposition of the phytoplankton monitoring requirements of Council Directive 91/492/EEC; - the updating of the establishments' lists, including the actual delisting by the Ministry of Public Health of the dispatch/purification centre; - the corrective measures of the shortcomings previously identified in establishments by the CA and/or identified by the mission team should be followed up in the establishments visited during the mission and in all other establishments that were not visited but that may have similar shortcomings; - the major deficiencies found during the mission and not previously identified by the CA should be followed up in the establishments visited during the mission and in all other establishments that were not visited but that may have similar shortcomings; - laboratories performing analyses for establishments' own-checks should only use methods that are in accordance with the approval procedures and in particular to the NRL positive list of validated methods.

Live bivalve molluscs Bivalve molluscs, in particular Scallops, should only be placed on the market if they do not contain higher contaminant levels than those specified in Commission Regulation 466/2001/EC. Furthermore, the FASFC should keep 14 the Commission services informed of the results of contaminated Scallops and the measures taken whenever high levels of Cadmium are detected.

Fishery products During production and before they are released for human consumption, fish and FP must be subject to a visual inspection for the purpose of detecting and removing any parasites that are visible in accordance to the requirements of Council Directive 91/493/EEC and Commission Decision 93/140/EEC. Whenever fish is sampled for histamine analysis, the sampling procedure to be followed by the CA should be the one required by Council Directive 91/493/EEC. 15 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7561/2005 All the recommendations on the report have been addressed by the Belgium CCA's communication to the FVO of 29 July 2005. It included details of corrective actions already undertaken and other planned actions, in particular: - Generalities: actions planned to be implemented during the months of September (e.g. VMM protocol and letter) and October 2005 (e.g. follow-up inspection s to vessels); - Live bivalve molluscs: September 2005 (i.e. use of mice in NRL for marine biotoxins); periodic reporting to the Commission of the heavy metals results of analysis carried out in scallops; - Fishery products: as from 2006, parasite checks will also be mandatory in the retail trade.
The competent authority should report to the European Commission in accordance with Article 2.1 of Commission Regulation (EC) No. 835/2004 on action taken with regard to essential uses.

The competent authorities should consider identifying the exact quantities of obsolete pesticides and arranging for their safe destruction, in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment.

It is advised to achieve clear delineation of responsibilities for pesticide residue analysis, and to establish co-ordination between residue monitoring activities by the involved competent authorities.

A co-ordinated national monitoring programme for pesticide residues, specifying at least the products to be inspected, the number of inspections to be carried out, the pesticide residues to be inspected and the criteria applied in drawing up these programmes, should be established in accordance with Article 2.1.a of Council Directive 90/642/EEC, and forwarded to the European Commission.
Sampling for pesticide residue analysis should be performed in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC, and inspectors should be trained in sampling requirements.

The competent authorities should consider increasing the range of pesticides and metabolites in the analytical screens, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and to ensure adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC as amended. 22

Accreditation of the laboratories carrying out pesticide residue analysis to ISO 17025 should be ensured. The laboratories should consider taking measures to avoid possible cross-contamination between standards and samples. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. In particular, they should intensify the supervision in those establishments where major non-compliances were present and ensure proper enforcement of corrective action.

As far as the controls regarding the use of WRA are concerned, the project which they intend to carry out in 2005 should take into account Commission Recommendation 2005/175/EC concerning a co-ordinated programme for the official controls of foodstuffs for 2005. The project should, therefore, include a calculation of the quantity of added water.

When the CA observe non-compliances in the use of WRA, either during the implementation of the 2005 WRA project or during other inspection activities, they should take the necessary enforcement actions. 14 ADDENDUM In their letter dated 23 November 2005, the CCA provided some information regarding corrective actions taken to address the recommendations made in the draft report. In particular, with regard to: Recommendations 5.1 and 5.2, they stated that the shortcomings identified were rectified immediately. In this context, the CA stated also, with regard to the practice of washing carcasses before the post-mortem inspection, covered implicitly by recommendation 5.2, that they have brought this point to the attention of the industry. The CA should ensure that fishing vessels are regularly inspected and that vessels equipped for chilling of FP are registered in accordance with Annex II, point 9 of Council Directive 92/48/EEC.
The CA should ensure a check on the conditions of landing and first sale in accordance with Chapter V, I, 2 of the Annex to Council Directive 91/493/EEC.

The CA should ensure that each batch of FP are submitted for inspection including organoleptic checks carried out by sampling before first sale as prescribed in Chapter V, II, 1 of the Annex to Council Directive 91/493/EEC.

The CA should improve the supervision of FP establishments and ensure that only establishments which are fully in compliance with the requirements of the Council Directive 91/493/EEC are on the list 11 of approved establishments. The CA should ensure that FP establishments only carry out activities for which they are approved.

The CA should ensure that own-checks, including HACCP plans, are properly assessed regarding compliance with Article 6 of Council Directive 91/493/EEC and Commission Decision 94/356/EC. Own- check testing should be carried out only in laboratories approved by the CA, in accordance with Article 6, 2nd subparagraph, 3rd indent of Council Directive 91/493/EEC.

The CA should ensure that testing for histamine is carried out in accordance with Chapter V, II, 3, A, (b) of the Annex to Council Directive 91/493/EEC. To ensure the full application of the national monitoring programme for brucellosis in cattle by improving awareness among farmers to notify abortions, by strengthening the official controls with regard to the application of relevant cross-checks and to apply relevant controls, such as cross-checks, in order to ensure that CSF examination of wild boars is carried out as required.

To amend the disease contingency plans for FMD, CSF, AI and ND in order to bring them fully into line with Council Directives 2003/85/EC, 2001/89/EC, 92/40/EEC and 92/66/EEC. 17 ADDENDUM Response of the Czech Authorities to the draft mission report The Czech Authorities offered comments on the draft report by means of a letter dated 16 December 2005. Where appropriate these comments have been incorporated into the final report. They also provided an initial reaction to certain conclusions a s in the report, in particular by providing details of action already taken or to be taken to correct deficiencies noted. A summary of these is indicated below: Recommendation 6.4. The system of checks, including recording and evaluation methods of animal welfare at slaughter will be evaluated in a meeting with the RVA inspectors by the end of 2005. Recommendation 6.7. A new system of notification of abortions to the control database has been introduced, enabling the SVA to check the notifications directly. All RVAs have been instructed to arrange for cooperation with the hunting association as regards trichinosis in feral pigs. Recommendation 6.8. Positive serological results of the vaccination of wild boars will be notified from the Slovak authorities on a monthly basis. However, due to the fact that a marker vaccine is not used in Slovakia, the Czech authorities cannot differentiate the antibodies. Recommendation 6.9. The methodology of CSF monitoring is updated by the SVA annually. The disease contingency plans have been amended concerning strategy of vaccination, information of population density, killing methodologies and certain annexes with regard to Council Directives 93/119/EEC, 92/40/EEC and 92/66/EEC respectively. The SVI, Brno is withdrawn from the list of laboratories for AI diagnosis.

Generalities related to CA FP/LBM control system performance Fishing vessels should comply with the requirements of Council Directive 92/48/EEC. The frequency of inspections carried out by the CA on fishing vessels and landing sites in order to verify their compliance should correspond to the one established by themselves and adequate numbers of staff to deal with this duty should be made available. The deficiencies found during the mission and not previously identified by the CA should be corrected in the establishments and dispatch centre visited and in all other establishments that were not visited but that may have similar shortcomings.

Live bivalve molluscs The classification of production areas should be amended according to microbiology results of monitoring. Provision for suspension in case of noncompliant results should be considered and possible conflicts of interest of the private entrepreneurs responsible for the collection of samples should be avoided. The NRL for microbiology should take contact with the Community Reference Laboratory in order to evaluate if procedures concerning the processing of samples (pooling and averaging) and interpretation of test data are appropriate. Further to this evaluation, the NRL should advise the state laboratories and the manual of procedures should be amended. Germany should respect the current Community requirements regarding the detection of marine biotoxins; therefore, in absence of validation of the chemical methods used, bioassays must be used. All the official laboratories performing chemical methods for the biotoxin identification should implement alternative detection methods able to detect DTX3. Adequate staff should be made available to the biotoxins NRL to enable it to adequately complete its assigned tasks. The deficiencies identified in laboratories, accredited by accreditation bodies, involved in official controls and own-checks should be rectified.

Fishery products Each batch of fishery products must be submitted for inspection (comprising an organoleptic check) by the CA at the time of landing or before first sale to determine, its fitness for human consumption. During production and before they are released for human consumption, fish and FP must be subject to a visual inspection for the purpose of detecting and removing any parasites that are visible in accordance with the requirements of Council Directive 91/493/EEC and Commission Decision 93/140/EEC. Whenever fish is sampled for official control of histamine, the sampling procedure to be followed by the CA should be the one required under Council Directive 91/493/EEC (nine samples must be taken from each batch). 19 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7583/2005 A reply to the FVO letter dated 18 November 2005 (ref. 5, paragraph 1) was sent by the CCA informing that the competent Ministry of the Federal State of Schleswig Holstein has corrected the procedure of production area classification in order to comply with Community requirements. In their comments to the draft report, (letter of 22 February 2006, ref: 106-3612- 01/234738), the CA provided some details of corrective actions already undertaken and other planned actions, in particular: - Generalities: in MV the inspection system concerning fishing vessels has now been changed. All fishing vessels supplying approved establishments are registered as being subject to inspection. Every inspection is documented. - The frequency of inspections carried out by the CA of MV on fishing vessels and landing sites in order to verify their compliance was fixed at once a year on the basis of a risk assessment. - The deficiencies found during the mission and not previously identified by the CA have been partially corrected in the establishment listed as No. 3 in Annex III of this report (deadline was set for 30 June 2006 for remedying all deficiencies). Deficiencies found in establishments No. 1, 2 and in the establishment processing bivalve molluscs of Annex III have been rectified. - Live bivalve molluscs: in respect of recommendation 5.2.paragraph 3, the NRL organised validation of methods tests for PSP amongst the official laboratories in Germany in 2004. The results were discussed in December 2004 and the methodological instructions were revised in December 2005 and are to be published in the summer of 2006 as the official method in §64 LFGB (Food and Feed Code - Collection of Methods). The CCA referred as well to the comments on bioassay under point 2.2.2.1.f of the report. Furthermore, they stated that an enquiry as to the suitability of MBA was sent to the EFSA (EFSA-Q-2005-285). A reply is expected in December 2006. - In respect of recommendation 5.2, paragraph 4, the CCA pointed out that the detection of toxins in the DSP group, including DTX-3, is currently a priority in the § 64 LFGB working party on mollusc toxins. - In respect of recommendation 5.2, paragraph 5, the CA stated that priority has been given to remedying the shortage of personnel and optimising the installations. - Fishery products: in respect of recommendation 5.3.paragraph 1 and 2 the CA of MV stated that during routine inspections of fishing vessels, landing sites in wholesale installations or processing establishments the criteria for freshness of the fish are now being documented - In respect of recommendation 5.3, paragraph 3, the CA provided documentation confirming that instructions were given to comply with Community requirements (nine samples must be taken from each batch) in the three Länder visited. 11/04/06 - 55332

The HR legislation on PH control for FP intended for export to the EU should be reviewed in order to include certain provisions at least equivalent to those required in Council Directive 91/493/EEC, in particular concerning the temperature of transport of FP (Directive 91/493/EEC, Annex, Chapter VIII, Point 1, 1st indent) and the requirements for RSW vessels (Directive 92/48/EEC, Annex 2, point 8);

ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7594/2005 In response to the recommendations in the draft report, the CAs indicated the followi s under point 8: With regard to the findings or deficiencies detected during the mission carried out last February, CCA have begun to rectify some of the general problems. (1) Directive 99/2002/EC and the provisions for the implementation of Regulation 998/2002/EC were transposed into Polish law by the Act dated 7 January 2005 amending the Act on the protection of animal health and on combating infectious diseases in animals, and amending various other acts (Official Gazette No 23, item 188) and by the Decree of the "Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development" dated 6 April 2005 concerning the production and placing on the market of various products of animal origin (currently being published in the Official Gazette). The provisions of Decision 2000/571/EC were incorporated into the CVO Instruction No GIWbip-2/2005 of 28 January 2005, as amended by Instruction No GIWbip-3/2005 of 28 February 2005.

Polish statutory provisions regarding veterinary border controls have been brought fully into line with Community legislation, and the Tables of Correspondence relating to the legal acts concerned have been accepted by the European Commission. The GVI has made every effort to ensure their proper implementation and enforcement in accordance with the recommendations of the FVO.

The CVO asked the "Ministry of Environment", by letter dated on 18 April (ref. GIWbip 20), to make some essential changes comprising the removal from the register of those border crossings where it is not possible to check live animals, and to leave only the possibility of CITES products being imported through them. The updated list is being sent to all Border Veterinary Officers and to the Head of Customs with the request that it be forwarded to the territorially competent Customs Departments at the border crossing points on the EU's external border.

The draft Decree of the "Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development" concerning a list of border crossing points at which customs bodies carry out checks on pets accompanying travellers and being transported for non- commercial purposes, and concerning the conditions and type of cooperation between customs bodies and District Veterinary Officers in the performance of those checks, is currently at the interdepartmental consultation stage. It is scheduled for publication in the Official Gazette in the first half of June 2005.

The GVI has drawn up training themes for official veterinarians working at BIPs and a training schedule for 2005. The subjects cover Community and national legislation in the field of border veterinary controls, as well as the Code of Administrative Procedure. The CVO has submitted an application to the TAIEX Bureau for the financing of practical training of official veterinarians at border crossing points in other Member States on a study-visit basis. Applications have also been submitted for the organisation of training in the form of workshops. From 18 to 21 and from 25 to 28 April 2005, training is being held for official veterinarians in the fields of equine identification, registration and welfare. The participants are six veterinarians from six BIPs approved for checks on category E animals and two members of staff from the Border Office of the GVI. 16

A working meeting was held at the "Ministry of Finance" on 8 March and 15 April 2005 of central and local representatives of the Customs Service and representatives of the GVI, the "Inspectorate for the Commercial Quality of Agricultural Food Products" and the "Sanitary Inspectorate". The purpose of the meeting was to identify all problems relating to cooperation between all the services carrying out checks at border crossing points. The Border Veterinary Officers were obliged by the CVO to organise similar meetings at local level, with the minutes of those meetings having to be submitted to the CVO. Customs have been provided with the current list of goods which are subject to veterinary inspection (Decision 2002/349). After CVO request in letter (ref. GIWbip 15, dated 16.02.2005) work on inclusion of the list of goods in the ISZTAR-II and CELINA system has already started, and the CVO will be notified as soon as the work has been completed. The question of cooperation in the field of checks on travellers' luggage will be settled under the agreement drawn up between the Head of Customs and the CVO. The CVO also sent a letter (dated 25 February, ref. GIWbip 403/mk-14/2005) to the Head of Customs proposing that joint training be organised relating to border checks on pets in accordance with the Act of 7 January 2005 amending the Act on the protection of animal health and on combating infectious diseases in animals and amending various other acts (Official Gazette No 23, item 188). Training of this kind has already been organised by the Border Veterinary Officers at a number of border crossing points, including at Warsaw Okecie Airport and the road border crossing point at Dorohusk and Bezledy. The training organised by the GVI and the Customs Department of the "Ministry of Finance" is scheduled for the last week of May. There will be 15 participants designated by the "Ministry of Finance" and the District Veterinary Officers territorially responsible for border crossing points at which checks are carried out on pets from third countries. In the Gynia and Bezledy the veterinary inspectors are allowed to open consignments without presence of the customs officer.

The GVI Border Office has drawn up a schedule of checks to be carried out in 2005 at the BIPs and customs warehouses approved for the inspection of products not meeting EU import requirements. They are to be carried out by Border Office inspectors either independently or in conjunction with staff of the GVI Inspections Office. In line with the recommendations made by the FVO, an amended Instruction of the Chief Veterinary Officer, GIWbip1/2005, has been issued, setting out the rules for granting and withdrawing approval for veterinary border inspection posts Concerning the BIP in the Port of Gdansk the CCA provided the information that these facilities are nearly completed, and in May 2005 the building will be inspected for acceptance by the individual departments and handed over for the use of the Border Veterinary Officer. On 12 April 2005, a GVI representative made an inspection visit after which comments a s were sent to the investor

On 11-12 April 2005, checks were carried out on customs warehouses in Gdynia included on the official list of warehouses approved for non-EU conforming products. The checks were performed by inspectors from the GVI 17 Border Office, with the participation of representatives of the Regional and District Veterinary Inspectorates. A post-inspection report was drawn up specifically addressing all the deficiencies noted and ordering their rectification by the end of May 2005. All approval decisions issued by the District Veterinary Officer for customs warehouses coming under his supervision were examined by the GVI Organisational and Legal Office for compliance with Community and national law. It is planned to carry out checks on all remaining customs warehouses and to organise training in the second half of May jointly with the customs services in the port of Gdynia with the aim of exchanging information on the subject of management and supervision of customs warehouses in general and, in particular, of customs warehouses, free customs zones and entities providing means of international transport within the meaning of veterinary and customs law. Every company engaged in supplying vessels with non-EU-conforming products has been informed about the need to obtain approval from GVI. There are currently no suppliers who use non-EU-conforming products for supplying international means of transport.

A plan for monitoring residues, pathogens and contaminants in products of animal origin imported from third countries and intended for use as foodstuffs has been drawn up in accordance with Regulation No 136/2004 by the GVI. Also drawn up was a plan for monitoring residues, contaminants and pathogens in animal feed. It was sent to the BIPs by letter of 18 April (ref. GIWpuf.512pi/50/2005)

The majority of deficiencies noted for facilities, equipment, hygiene, documentation, registration and records in Gdynia and Bezledy have been rectified, and the remaining ones will be eliminated by the deadline set by the FVO. Detailed information was given in Annex 1 of the letter GIW ie 860/13a BIP/2005 dated on 25 April 2005.

The CCA did not indicate a response to the recommendation concerning checks of the products of non-animal origin except hay and straw.

An amended version of the Border Veterinary Officers' Manual was drawn up at the Border Office and sent to all BIPs as a set of guidelines for the conduct of inspections by official veterinarians. As part of the inspection process, all deficiencies or matters of doubt are the subject of ongoing correction on the basis of post-inspection reports.

Jointly with the Ministry of Finance, the GVI has drawn up the wording of an agreement between the CVO and the Head of Customs setting out the rules governing checks on the travellers' luggage of travellers from third countries in accordance with Regulation No 745/2005. Under the agreement, it is the customs services which check travellers' luggage for imported products of animal origin. Seized foodstuffs are placed in locked seized-goods containers which are clearly marked as such. The customs services send information on seized products to the territorially competent District or Border Veterinary Officer. The manager of the border crossing point is responsible for sending the contents of the seized-goods containers to category II disposal facilities. The CVO has also sent a letter to the Chairman of the National Tourist Council at the Ministry of Economy and Labour with the aim of informing tourist organisations about requirements relating to the import of animal-origin products in travellers' luggage. The Embassies of Belarus, Russia and the Ukraine have been informed, and a multimedia presentation has been placed on the official GVI website. On 14 March 2005, an agreement was signed between the Director of the Customs Department at Bezledy and the Border Veterinary Officer "concerning activities relating to checks on the import of animal-origin products in travellers' luggage". On 3 February 2005, the Border Office sent updated posters complying with Regulation No 745/2004 to the Warminsko-Mazurskie Regional Authority in Olsztyn, which forwarded them to the manager of the border crossing point at Bezledy. The posters were put up at the border crossing point in the first half of March 2005. In order to organise checks on travellers' luggage at border crossings where there is no approved BIP, the CVO sent a letter dated 25 February (ref. GIWbip 19) to the territorially competent Regional Veterinary Officers with a view to information being passed on to the District Veterinary Officers and appropriate agreements with the customs services being signed.

The CVO has written to all Border Veterinary Officers (ref. GIWbip 30) instructing them to stop accepting heath certificates for products of animal origin which are in transit or coming from temporary storage on the EU territory and which do not satisfy the standards applying since 1 January 2005. The procedures have been amended and consignments from Russia to third countries are not dispatched under the same conditions as transit within Russia. 19

The Border Veterinary Officer at Bezledy has terminated the waste-disposal contract with the incinerator facility of the District Hospital, because it did not have approval for the processing of category 1 materials. A new agreement is to be signed on 1 June 2005 with a production and trading company , which is approved for the processing of category 1 materials under Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002. The other BIPs have waste-disposal agreements exclusively with operators approved under Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002. Inspection of kitchen waste from international means of transport is performed by the "Environmental Protection Department of the Marine Board". The district Veterinary Officer receives a report from the Marine Board on the volume of waste which has been delivered to an approved storage site and its copy is forwarded to the Border Veterinary Officer. .

Uniformity between the regional food and veterinary authorities will be achieved by issuing circulars and guidelines and holding meetings at which all inspection departments will be represented. The DVFA is planning to revise the guidelines on documentation of checks relating to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses by the end of 2006. In the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA highlighted the points to be followed for performing regular animal welfare audits and checks in slaughterhouses. · Regardi s n° 2 and n°3, the DVFA will ensure that checklists used in slaughterhouses are regularly updated and that check lists specific to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses are used during animal welfare inspections. Appropriate provisions on the stunning of animals will be included in the new guidelines on documentation of checks relating to animal welfare requirements at slaughterhouses and the previous outdated circular on stunning will be repealed before the end of 2006. In the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA highlighted the need for appropriate reporting and recording of the results of animal welfare audits and inspections. · Regardi n°3 on training, the DVFA will ensure regular training on animal welfare in slaughterhouses for all official veterinarians. welfare requirements. · Regardi n° 4, in the letters addressed to the heads of the regional authorities on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests from the head of the region concerned that it should be ensured in connection with re-approval of the slaughterhouse that the slope of entry and exit ramps should be kept to the minimum possible. · Regardi n° 5, in the letters addressed to the heads of two regions concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that the slaughterhouses be informed in writing that animals which are not taken directly to the place of slaughter must have access to drinking water and that compliance with this requirement must be checked. · Regardi n° 6, in a letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA requests that it should be ensured that the slaughterhouse puts in place a procedure to avoid unnecessary excitement to the broilers kept in cages before slaughter and during washing at the slaughterhouse. 23 · Regardi n°7, in the letter addressed to the head of the region concerned on 1 June 2006, the DVFA request that it should be ensured that the slaughterhouse is informed in writing that animals must be handled by persons with the necessary knowledge and skills, and be spared any avoidable excitement during handling. · Regardi n° 8, the DVFA stated that the stunning device was fitted with visible signal and that the operator demonstrated to the mission team that the light lit up when there was current between electrodes in a bucket of water. · Regardi n° 9, in the letter addressed to the head of the regions Legislation New legislation and implementing provisions were issued to address the recommendations issued with mission report 7676/2005, in line with the commitments made by Lithuania before the Standing Committee in December 2005. A correct meaning of "other fields" as mentioned in Council Directive 93/85/EEC has been introduced by the Order No 3D-87 and implemented consistently, addressing Recommendation (2) of report DG(SANCO)7676/2005. 7.2. Plant health system in Lithuania The SPPS headquarters has a good level of control of the activities performed for potato controls. Inspectors met were competent and acquainted with the new provisions on potato controls. A good level of awareness of producers, wholesalers and managers of packing stations on ring rot issues was noted during the on-the-spot visits. Activities on potato controls are carried out consistently in the regions visited. 7.3. Seed potatoes in Lithuania Plant passports for seed potatoes are now being issued; labels and information contained are in compliance with Commission Directive 92/105/EEC. The potato genetic material originating in Third Countries detained by the Lithuanian Institute of Agriculture will be tested in 2007 for all the organisms mentioned in Commission Directive 95/44/EC, before its release, as requested by Recommendation (6). Checks are performed by the SPPS where seed potatoes are traded for the presence of the plant passport. 7.4. Potatoes other than seed All potato growers who want to trade their production need to be registered with the SPPS, as well as packing stations and wholesalers. The number of registered producers has almost doubled since last mission. The registration of producers is still in progress. 18 Handling of ring rot outbreaks is done in compliance with the requirements of Council Directive 93/85/EC: procedures, demarcation of zones and official measures are applied consistently, as requested by Recommendation (1). The incidence of the disease has increased compared to previous year: this is mainly due to the inclusion of small farms in the national survey. Quarantine measures applied following an outbreak are compulsory and if necessary are enforced, addressing Recommendation (3). The legal owners of fields subject to quarantine measures are informed about the measures imposed on them following an occurrence of a quarantine organism, as requested by Recommendation (4). Labels attached to ware potatoes include a registration number in accordance with the requirements of point 18.5 of Annex IV, part A, Section II to Council Directive 2000/29/EC, and as indicated by Recommendation (5). A list of varieties accepted as being resistant to potato wart disease and potato cyst nematode was sent by Lithuania to the Commission, in compliance with Article 10 of Council Directives 69/464/EEC and 69/465/EEC, as requested by Recommendation (7). Non registered producers are included in the surveys and controls for ring rot, addressing Advisory point (9). Occasional checks are performed by the SPPS at open markets to check for compliance with the provisions for labelling. 7.5. Laboratories Despite the fact that the new laboratory will only be completed later this year, the number of analyses performed for ring rot has increased substantially. The density of laboratory testing for ring rot has been increased and includes farm saved seed, as indicated in Advisory point (8). The requirements for water sampling for potato brown rot testing is now in line with the ones in the note on included sampling in the proposed amendment to Council Directive 98/57/EC14 , as requested by Advisory point (10). 7.6. Recommendation from report DG(SANCO)7261/2005 Recommendations (3) and (4) issued with mission report DG(SANCO)7261/2005 have been satisfactorily addressed. 14 SANCO/1191/2004 Rev. 9 (PVNA/2004/1191/1191R9-EN.doc) 19 8. OVERALL CONCLUSION The actions taken for the control of potato ring rot, disease caused by the bacterium Clavibacter michiganensis ssp. sepedonicus, are now in compliance with those established in Council Directive 93/85/EC. Procedures were found to be implemented homogeneously throughout the country. Official measures and disposal of contaminated potatoes are done under the supervision of the State Plant Protection Service. Plant passport for seed potatoes is now being issued. All recommendations of the report DG(SANCO)7676/2005 and recommendations (3) and (4) of mission report DG(SANCO)7261/2004 have been satisfactorily addressed. 9. text: To further enhance the operational value of data included in the identification and registration system for sheep and goats and to introduce checks in this area in compliance with Regulation (EC) No 1505/2006, so as to: - allow an appropriate and regular monitoring of progress in the epidemio- surveillance of TSEs required by Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, and - support the eradication of TSEs required by Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To take measures to increase the rate of notification of animals suspected of being infected by a TSE, as required by Art. 11 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, in particular by providing the education programmes laid down in (20) It has to be noted that this part of the overall conclusion reflects the legal situation at the time of the mission, which pre-dates the suspension by the Court of First Instance of certain provisions of Regulation (EC) No 727/2007 referred to in footnote No 11. 16 Art. 10 of the same Regulation for keepers of small ruminant flocks (other than those already confirmed as infected with a TSE).

To ensure compliance with requirements for sampling and testing of dead animals in order to bring epidemio-surveillance for TSEs in line with targets set up in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and, in particular, to accelerate detection of all possible TSE infected flocks.

To ensure that the NRL has the capacity to perform all diagnostic and confirmatory tests for TSEs in small ruminants necessary to comply with provisions in this respect laid down in Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To ensure that when a TSE is officially suspected in an ovine or caprine animal, all other ovine and caprine animals at the holding are placed under official movement restriction in compliance with Art. 12 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and no animal can be slaughtered for human consumption until the results of the analysis of the suspected case are available.

To ensure that once a TSE case is confirmed, discriminatory tests are carried out in line with provisions laid down in Annex X (Chapter C) to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 in order to exclude the presence of BSE in the infected flock.

To ensure that alternative eradication measures to killing and destruction of all animals present in a flock where a TSE is confirmed, in particular those allowing slaughtering of any of these animals for human consumption, are only applied when the presence of BSE can be excluded in the infected flock, as laid down in Annex VII (Chapter A) to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001

To enhance verification of compliance with requirements of the national sheep breeding programme for resistance to TSEs in order to ensure that it is applied in line with Art. 6a and Annex VII (Chapter B) to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To enhance verification of official controls on removal, handling and disposal of SRM in all places where they are produced in accordance to Art. 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 so as to ensure effective application of provisions laid down in Annex V to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To introduce official controls in accordance to Art. 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in order to ensure that the ban on trading with other Member States set out in Art. 1 of Decision 2007/315/EC is complied with. 9. COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

In case of findings of Ralstonia solanacearum, the extent of probable contamination is determined in accordance with Article 5(1)(a)(iii) of Council Directive 98/57/EC, and any plant material determined as probably contaminated is disposed of as specified in Article 6(2) of the same Directive.

In case of findings of Ralstonia solanacearum, the extent of the contamination is determined in accordance with Article 5(1)(a)(i) of Council Directive 98/57/EC, in particular that surface water is considered as an element in the investigation, as specified in Annex IV of the same Directive.

Official surveys for Bursaphelenchus xylophilus are conducted, as required by Article 4(1) of Commission Decision 2006/133/EC, on susceptible wood and bark and susceptible plants originating in Greece, to determine whether there is any evidence of infestation by this pest. Official surveys for Phytophthora ramorum in Greece are conducted, as required by Article 6(1) of Commission Decision 2002/757/EC. The results of those surveys are notified to the Commission and to the other Member States by 1 November of each year, as required by Article 6(2) of the same Decision. 41

Official surveys for the presence of Diabrotica virgifera in areas in Greece, where maize is grown, are conducted, as required by Article 2(1) of Commission Decision 2003/766/EC. Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005). The CA should ensure that FCI contains all the information required by EU legislation (see Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

The CCA should ensure the correct implementation of SNCPs by carrying out internal or external audits of the regional/municipal services involved as required by point 6 of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
The CCA should ensure that the CAs have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls in order to fulfil the requirements of Articles 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The CA should ensure that adequate biosecurity standards are in place in all poultry farms, in line with the Point 4(h), Part A (II), Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and in line with the SNCPs.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in breeding flocks complies fully with the requirements of Regulations (EC) No 2160/2003 and (EU) No 200/2010, in particular regarding sampling frequency, sampling protocol used and confirmatory sampling.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in laying flocks is fully compliant with the requirements of Regulation (EU) No 517/2011, in particular regarding sampling protocol used and confirmatory sampling policy.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in turkey breeding flocks complies fully with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and 584/2008, in particular as regards sampling frequency and sampling protocol used.

The CCA should ensure that the designated NRL for Salmonella organises proficiency testing and ensures an appropriate follow-up of such tests as required by Article 33 (2c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in breeding flocks complies fully with the requirements of Regulations (EC) No 2160/2003 and (EU) No 200/2010, in particular regarding confirmatory sampling.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in laying flocks is fully compliant with the requirements of Regulations (EC) No 2160/2003 and (EU) No 517/2011, in particular regarding sampling protocol used during food-borne outbreak investigations and regarding confirmatory sampling policy.

The CCA should ensure that the content of the FCI complies fully with the requirements of Section III of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and point 4.2 of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 200/2012, in particular results of any analysis carried within the framework of SNCPs is included.

The CCA should notify to Commission services and Member States the national legislation establishing the rules governing the activities and persons involved in the direct supply, by the producer, of small quantities of meat from poultry and lagomorphs slaughtered on the farm to the final consumer or to local retail establishments directly supplying such meat to the final consumer as fresh meat ( see Article 1.3(d) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004), as required by Directive 98/34/EC and Article 17(5) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The CA should ensure that official controls are effective enough to detect all the deficiencies in the establishments ( point 2(a), Chapter II of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in laying flocks is fully compliant with the requirements of Regulations (EC) No 2160/2003 and (EU) No 517/2011, in particular regarding routine confirmatory sampling policy, frequency in FBO and official sampling and confirmatory sampling protocol applied.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in broilers flocks is fully compliant with the requirements of Regulations (EC) No 2160/2003 and (EU) No 200/2012, in particular regarding frequency of official sampling and food chain information on Salmonella test results.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in turkey breeding flocks complies fully with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and 584/2008, in particular regarding routine confirmatory sampling policy, official sampling frequency and status of sampling and FBO sampling protocol used.

The CCA should ensure that the monitoring and sampling programme applied in fattening turkeys complies fully with the requirements of Regulations (EC) Nos 2160/2003 and 584/2008, in particular regarding routine confirmatory sampling policy, official sampling frequency and status of sampling.

Ensure that all retailers selling organic products to the final consumer have submitted their undertaking to the control system as required by Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

As already recommended in report DG(SANCO) 2009-8263 (Recommendation one), the CCA should ensure that training for official veterinarians, including in particular those working at exit points, meets the requirement of Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 concerning the recording equipment for road transport and the satellite navigation system so that checks on these are implemented. ure efficient and effective co-ordination of the monitoring and official controls on dioxins and PCBs in fish and fishery products from the Baltic sea by competent authorities at central level, the Länder and the municipalities as required by Article 4.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2004/882.

ure that the requirements for establishments in Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 for HACCP based procedures are fulfilled by food business operators. In particular, biotoxins, purification, smoking and cooking processes and have to be properly described in the relevant HACCP plans.

Research and emerging technologies Findings 19. One of the research institutes met during the remote part of the study is working in partnership with a university on a project (NatiMon) to collect indicators and parameters for determining animal welfare in rainbow trout and carp farms.: · This project aims at creating the basis for a regular and harmonised indicator-based animal welfare monitoring for key aquaculture species. · The identified welfare indicators are ­ preliminarily ­ mortality, dissolved oxygen levels, morphological conditions of the fish (e.g. skin or eye problems, fin or body lesions) and swimming behaviour. · The project is expected to be completed in 2023 and will result in the publication of guidance brochures ­ one for carp and one for trout ­ to assist stakeholders in identifying, measuring and assessing the welfare indicators on the aquaculture farm. · The project will not establish ranges or limits to determine satisfactory levels of welfare in the farms. 20. One of the associations met during the remote part of the study published a guidance document `Animal welfare indicators' to assist fish farmers in the practical implementation of their own checks. This document provides indicative water quality parameters to be met for salmonid and carp welfare, and possible corrective measures that 7 can be taken to address related issues. However, none of the farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study were measuring these parameters. 21. Research and competent authority representatives agreed that dissolved oxygen is the most important water quality parameter to monitor for fish welfare. 22. The long-distance transporter visited during the on-the-spot part of the study had collaborated to a project (Fish Transport Project ­ FiT) aimed at developing a mobile fish transport system with integrated water treatment. The system developed significantly reduces the carbon dioxide concentration in the water thus improving water quality and fish welfare during transport.

Quality assurance schemes and fish farmers' own checks Findings 23. In their reply to the pre-mission questionnaire, the competent authorities did not identify any quality scheme specifically promoting the welfare of farmed fish. 24. Qualified veterinary services visit farms on a regular basis due to animal health EU requirements. One of these services ­ met during the on-the-spot visits to the fish aquaculture farms ­ can measure oxygen saturation and temperature levels in the water for fish health reasons.: · These parameters could also serve as animal welfare indicators. Currently they do not record the general morphological conditions of the fish (mortalities, skin or eye problems, fin or body lesions). · This qualified service is drafting a protocol ­ based on the results of the NatiMon project ­ to record lesions that would indicate animal welfare or animal health issues and to check other animal welfare indicators. 25. Fish farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study indicated that the main welfare indicator they assess is mortality but that they would record this only when it exceeds normal daily mortality. Article 186(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on transmissible animal diseases requires the farms visited to keep mortality records in any case. · Farmers rearing the same fish species in similar conditions each gave a significantly different value to "normal daily mortality". · Only one of the farms visited kept mortality records, including the numbers and total weight of dead fish. This is considered a good practice, as it provides an idea of the production stage of the fish concerned. · The other farmers had empty mortality records although there had been disease outbreaks in their farms. In one case, the farmer had recently requested the intervention of the Fish Health Service because of high mortalities throughout a full week but had not recorded these in the mortality sheet. 8 26. Stakeholders met during the remote part of the study indicated that monitoring and measuring animal welfare indicators becomes increasingly relevant with increasing intensity and technology of the farming system. 27. Operators transporting fish (mainly on short journeys) identify oxygen saturation as the critical water quality factor to ensure fish welfare during transport. 28. Farmers are generally stunning the fish using a percussive blow to the head before bleeding them. 5.3 CHALLENGES FACED 29. Fish farmers met during the on-the-spot part of the study indicated that their main welfare concern is the prevention of predators as these kill and injure the fish they are keeping. 30. The stakeholders met during the study and a representative from one of the States' competent authorities indicated that they would disagree with establishing generic limits for most welfare parameters since these limits would vary depending on the production systems, fish species and their life stages. 31. The representative of one of the producers' associations met during the remote part of the study indicated that there is limited access to private veterinarians specialised in aquaculture health and production. This is causing delays in obtaining timely diagnoses and, consequently, longer waiting times to provide suitable treatment to the fish. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION Germany has set up a system for official controls on the welfare of farmed fish. There are advisory documented procedures supporting the official controls on fish farms. National legislation in Germany requires fish farmers to measure and assess animal welfare indicators on their farms. However, there are generally no clearly defined limits for welfare indicators at farm in documented procedures nor in most guidance available. The exceptions are a recently developed documented procedure in one of the States visited and a guidance document produced by an association. This guidance provides indicative water quality parameters for salmonids and carp but fish farmers do not seem to be using it. Their welfare indicator of preference is mortality but in general farmers are not recording this, making it difficult for competent authorities to assess farms' own checks. Additionally, there is ongoing research to provide stakeholders with indicators and parameters for determining animal welfare in rainbow trout and carp farms. This would help fish farmers in managing fish welfare in their farms. German transporters consider dissolved oxygen levels in the water as the critical welfare indicator during transport. This is generally the only parameter they monitor and is done indirectly through the flow rate of oxygen pumped into the water. However, there is ongoing 9 research to control other water quality parameters during the journey, such as dissolved carbon dioxide. Currently, the fish aquaculture representatives would not want EU legislation on fish welfare that is not species, and production system, specific. The impact of predators is the main welfare concern to fish famers. 7 CLOSING MEETING The study team held a closing meeting on 31 May 2023 with representatives from the federal level and from the states visited, at which the main findings of the fact-finding study were presented.

The Directorate of Animal Welfare, Veterinary Medicinal Products and Veterinary Applications within the Veterinary Directorate-General of the Ministry of Rural Development and Food is the central competent authority (hereafter: competent authority) responsible for supervision and the coordination of delivering official controls of the welfare rules for farmed fish at all relevant stages of production. The local competent authorities of the regions deliver the official controls at farms and other establishments.

The national veterinary legislation sets, among others, the hygiene requirements for the foundation and operation of aquaculture establishments, regulates fish health and welfare and requirements up to the placement of safe products in the market. The approval of establishments as well as transporters of live fish is a task assigned to local veterinary competent authorities.

The competent authority has considered the Recommendation concerning Farmed Fish and formally ratified it. They have not incorporated it in the national legislation and therefore they did not issue further legal text. However, the inspection checklist includes a question about scientific protocols or guidance (including a reference to the Recommendation) used in the fish farm. In addition, parts of the Recommendation have been elaborated in the guidelines developed (paragraph 4). Those guidelines have been disseminated in the local competent authorities to be considered during the preparation and performance of official controls in fish farms. In addition, further reference to the Recommendation is made in the national guidance (paragraph 17). Other parts of the Recommendation are included in Presidential decree 28/2009.

The competent authority has developed a policy for farmed fish that identifies the need to examine the applied practices in the production with a focus on welfare in transport and slaughter. It aims to develop methodologies to enhance the existing legislation and also to contribute to the preparation of future legislation. In that context, with the support of the academia, they have participated in various projects on the application of alternative methods for fishing and slaughtering of fish. In addition, the competent authority coordinated the production of Guidelines on water quality and handling for the welfare of farmed vertebrate fish. The guidelines were produced in 2020 voluntarily under the EU Platform on Animal Welfare. These guidelines on water quality and on handling aim to be of use for aquaculture operators and the relevant competent authorities. They include factors and parameters that are common across species. The guidelines adopt and embed the Council of Europe Recommendation concerning farmed fish. 4

The competent authority considers the training of personnel crucial to enhance the welfare practices in farmed fish sector. In cooperation with academia, they have designed and implemented training for staff involved in fish farming as well training for official inspectors - the most recent ones in 2022 and 2023.

In the context of the project titled `Development of expertise for the review and update of the multi annual strategic plan for the development of aquaculture 2021-2027', the competent authority has identified the relevance and importance of fish welfare in the context of aquaculture development. Various research works exploring welfare issues are ongoing under this project. 5.1.2 Planning, methodology and delivery of the official controls Findings

The competent authority has made available to the local competent authorities a written procedure that defines the methodology for risk-based planning of the official controls. The methodology considers farmed fish as a stand-alone area, and it includes a separate tab for numerical calculation of the risk of each aquaculture establishment. Among other factors, the methodology lists the production size, the past record of official controls (existence of non-compliances), the likelihood of extreme weather temperatures, time elapsed since last official control, the turnover rate and competence of staff and the existence of certification under a quality assurance scheme. According to the methodology the farmed fish presents low risk related relating to animal welfare.

The local competent authorities perform official controls on animal welfare at fish farms in the context of fish health inspections. They use a joint checklist that includes fish health checks as well as a part dedicated to fish welfare. That part covers the use of scientifically proven protocols or guidelines to ensure welfare, the use of welfare indicators, the methods of stunning and killing of fish. In addition, it includes the verification of requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 for example vehicle transport authorisation and transporter licence. Apart from the part referring to live fish transport, the other points covered by the checklist do not relate to specific legal requirements and are thus not enforceable.

The manual for animal welfare checks during transport (second version, 2023), includes in Chapter 16 specific guidelines for fish transport that assist the inspectors in their work. It includes guidelines for the evaluation of transport vehicles before approval as well as during routine inspections, for example the assessment of fitness of fish to be transported, the loading practices etc.

One of the regions has prepared a comprehensive checklist that covers the inspection of essential elements of the system applied in a fish farm as well as different process steps. This checklist includes training requirements, monitoring of indicators and keeping of records, implementation of corrective actions, assessment of the environmental conditions (e.g. density, light, protective nets), feeding practices, stunning and killing. It goes beyond 5 legal requirements but is very informative on whether and how the fish farm addresses welfare of the fish.

Although the competent authority suggests a risk-based system for selecting fish farms for animal welfare official controls, this methodology was followed only in one of the three regions visited. In two regions visited there are annual inspections of farms including transport processes and vehicles, and in another region visited, there are official controls every three years as the farmed fish is ranked as of low risk compared to other sectors in that region.

The transport operation examined during the on-the-spot part of the study, was equipped with insulated water tanks and a system to monitor water temperature, oxygen and pH. They were also equipped with an alarm system for oxygen and with backup systems to supply oxygen in case of need. for pumping the oxygen into the water tanks.

Immersion in ice and water mix (ice slurry) to provoke thermal shock (hypothermia) and asphyxia is the killing method used in practice and does not include a stunning step. Electric stunning is a requirement under the organic standard (see paragraph 21) and is also used on a voluntary basis on ongoing experimental scale by some companies in cooperation with research institutes. It has been trialled with a view to anaesthetising fish rapidly and directly after they are pumped from cages prior to killing via immersion in ice baths. This technology, which is used for Atlantic salmon and on a small scale for rainbow trout and carp, is regarded as being in line with EU animal welfare objectives as using it guarantees immediate stunning prior to killing. However, the parameters that ensure proper anaesthesia for different species and different size of fish are not yet well known, indicating that more research needs to be done in that area. Electrical stunning presents a risk to operators and requires a significant amount of investment, as it must be done in the sea, on board modified vessels that reach the cages of fish. This means that the method might be of severe financial burden for small and medium size operators.

According to the competent authority, the most critical steps in the process concerning elevated risk to fish welfare are lack of or inadequate feeding, vaccination, exhaustion of breeding stock, improper stunning, handling during selection, stocking density (especially relating to reduced oxygen levels as well as difficulties in reaching feed), impact of parasitic diseases. 5.2 OTHER MEASURES TO PROTECT THE WELFARE OF FARMED FISH 5.2.1 Research and emerging technologies ­ Other initiatives Findings

As mentioned earlier in the report (paragraph 13) there are ongoing projects managed by academia in cooperation with fish farming companies related to stunning and slaughtering of fish based on alternative methods and electric stunning. This has led to the production 6 and optimisation of pumping systems, electric stunning and killing of fish on board vessels. The results have led to the production of documented procedures that instruct operators how to perform relevant tasks, and aspects to be considered with regards to protecting staff safety, optimising quality and yield of product, and ensuring adequate levels of welfare with reduced stress of fish. For example, it describes how to collect and pump the fish so that crowding and injuries are prevented.

The main objective of the research for alternative methods for fishing (stunning and slaughtering) is to optimise fish welfare. It aims to develop a biosensor to monitor fish cortisol levels based on a non-intervention method to evaluate the level of stress. The wider goal is to deploy the biosensor in assessing the stress of fish at different production steps including breeding and fattening.

The association of farmed fish producers has published a guidance document titled Mediterranean Fish Welfare: Guide to good practices and assessment indicators. The competent authority adopted the guide and disseminated it to all relevant competent authorities. Published in 2020, its main objectives are to describe current scientific data and ethical practices on animal welfare with particular focus on the needs of European sea bass and gilthead sea bream in different production phases, in relation to improving their welfare. It includes operational and laboratory welfare indicators and lists their advantages and disadvantages. It covers different production systems, production phases and husbandry practices.

In the case of Pagrus major farms the companies have installed tents to protect the cages from intense sunlight as it is proven that direct sunlight enhances the aggressive behaviour of the fish. However, as the farmers stated during the visit, this feature reduces the possibility to observe the fish. This highlights the complexity of welfare issues in the aquaculture sector.

During the visit, representatives from the fish farming companies as well as the association of farmed fish producers discussed the main indicators they are using that are relevant to welfare. They mainly monitor and assess mortality as well as a wide range of other parameters including density and environmental indicators (water temperature, oxygen etc). They also widely deploy observations of fish behaviour during handling and especially feeding to assess the welfare status of fish. A representative commented on the importance of monitoring the acute/dramatic change of indicators, especially mortality to trigger alerts on welfare or health status.

In one company visited, the quality department has developed an advanced indicator system to monitor deficiencies of received fish in the packing plant. This includes indicators of haematomas and similar issues that affect the quality and yield of the production. The association of farmed fish producers has also developed comprehensive photographic guidance to evaluate those deficiencies, including in addition to haematomas, a range of morphological deviations (injuries, absence of gills covers, malformed fish etc). Monitoring some of those indicators is a potentially good practice as 7 a useful tool not only to minimise quality defects, as but also for monitoring welfare as these parameters could also relate to welfare. At this stage however there is not adequate scientific evidence to suggest sufficient baseline levels within which welfare can be considered satisfactory. 5.2.2 Quality assurance schemes and fish farmers' own checks Findings

The competent authorities specified three quality schemes that include welfare requirements used in Greece within their applied scope. Those are an international standard applied in farmed fish, an international standard specifically for organic farmed fish and a national standard developed by the association of farmed fish producers. All three are promoting the welfare of farmed fish, they are accredited, and they are applied on a voluntary basis. They include sections with requirements relating to welfare of fish at the different stages of production. The standards include some specific requirements but mostly generic and open requirements. For example, requirements for the humane slaughter of fish, reduction of stress during handling and transport processes, training for staff involved in the production of fish, monitoring of health, requirements relating to feeding and quality of feeding stuff etc. They also include some specific requirements. · The international standard has established risk assessment for fish welfare as a major requirement. It is asking to conduct a risk assessment for fish welfare at all stages of production from the hatchery to stunning and killing of fish and to document/monitor proposed actions to mitigate those risks. The study team considers this as a potentially good practice if consistently applied in the farmed fish sector. · The organic standard requires that live fish must be supplied with enough oxygen during transport and when kept in cages. A transport density of 1 kg of fish per 8 litres of water may not be exceeded. The water must be changed at the latest after 6 hours of transport and must be of the same temperature. The transport duration is maximum 10 hours. In addition, slaughtering of fish shall be carried out by means of incision of gills or immediate evisceration. Prior to this, fish must be stunned by means of concussion, or electrocution. The standard sets requirements for density at farm for other species (e.g. for salmon) but not for sea bass and sea bream. · The national standard includes a section for welfare. It requires documented procedures and records to demonstrate protection of fish at all production stages, monitoring and control of fish mortality, monitoring of feeding quality and quantity, feed withdrawal times, the establishment and use of practices to reduce fish stress during handling processes etc. Twenty-one (out of twenty- two) members of the association are certified under the standard. This represents a total of 80% of the national production certified. The representatives of the association indicated that they plan to embed specific 8 requirements included in their published guidelines (paragraph 17) in the new version of the standard.

Representatives of competent authorities as well as operators met during the study indicated that the use of private quality schemes has been proven to be useful to enter markets and the companies have benefited in their operations by consistently applying documented procedures and standardising their processes. 5.3 CHALLENGES FACED

Local competent authorities indicated that their main challenges are the difficulty to perform official controls, as reaching farms in the sea depends on weather conditions and the long travel distance. The specialised knowledge required for fish welfare inspection presents a challenge for official inspectors dealing with controls of various sectors. In addition, the open/generic legal requirements combined with gaps in the available knowledge relating to scientifically established baselines on fish welfare limit the capacity to enforce.

The representatives of the producers' association and the academic institute as well as representatives from the producers met, also described the challenges they face concerning fish welfare. Primarily, the lack of available scientific knowledge limits the use of indicators to protect productivity/efficiency as it is not clear which levels are sufficient to ensure acceptable conditions for welfare. They also commented that the market of farmed fish is price-driven and the competition with non-EU producers is hard to follow. This is due to increased cost for EU producers to comply with EU standards not applicable to non-EU producers (namely, in addition to welfare, feed and management of animals by product requirements). In that respect, they commented that the current requirements for labelling do not support the fish produced in the EU. In addition, they questioned whether there are welfare standards applicable to wild caught fish. They would welcome the introduction of new legislation, but strictly on a species-specific basis, scientifically based, and applicable to both EU and non-EU producing countries that place products on the European market. As the current knowledge is not sufficient to support specific indicators/descriptive requirements, they suggest the introduction of qualitative/open requirements such as the obligation to keep staff trained and up to date on welfare issues, and specific tools such as the obligatory use of root cause analysis tools and reporting on welfare issues. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION The report finds that there is a system for official controls on the welfare of farmed fish in Greece. There are documented procedures supporting the official controls on fish farms and good knowledge of farmed fish welfare matters by both the central competent authority and industry. Official controls cover animal welfare in the context of fish health inspections. However, they have a reduced impact on welfare (apart from the 9 requirements for transport vehicles) as there are no legally enforceable requirements specific to fish welfare. Industry processes have several arrangements, established by joint efforts with the state, research institutes and the industry. This includes a national accredited private quality scheme, a guide to good practices on fish welfare linked to the certification scheme and a wide range of indicators already in use. Although indicators might cover welfare, they are predominantly used to ensure quality and efficiency of production. There is ongoing academic research determining welfare in sea bass and sea bream and other species farmed in the country to provide stakeholders with guidance and baselines for corresponding indicators. This, (the absence of welfare related baselines on indicators), is the main challenge that both competent authorities and operators face, and advances would help fish farmers in managing fish welfare in their farms. The study identified a good practice in a private quality assurance scheme that requires a documented risk assessment methodology to mitigate risks for animal welfare throughout the processes from hatchery to stunning and killing of fish, if applied consistently by the operators. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting took place on 20 September 2023 with representatives of the Commission and competent authorities at which the main findings of the fact-finding study were presented.
